original_chunks: Walking into the voting booth "...every four years on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November" (Office Of Federal Register 6), the people of the United States of America expect their vote to count.
Although, the president is elected in a more indirect way, by the electoral college, which does not represent the people, and is not fair.
The president should be chosen by a direct popular vote in the future.
The electoral college fails to genuinely reflect the people's opinion.
Voters might mistakenly vote for the wrong candidate due to confusion about electors (Plumer 10).
Not every voter is educated on exactly how the electors and candidates are represented on the ballot and that may lead to an accidental win.
Electors pledged to a candidate can change their vote, which may be misleading (Plumer 10).

Even Posner who writes for the electoral college admitted that it is possible, and he claims that it is "rare";however, it has happened before in 1960 (Plumer 11), and not even Posner can control the actions of an elector, legally anyway.
Also, when a candidate wins a popular vote, which is the true mind of the people, that candidate still may not win the electoral vote, overall, loosing the election.
This situation happened in the 2000 election between Bush and Gore (Posner 16).
The electoral college inherently produces unjust elections.
The first example appears in the method of the "..."winner-take-all" system that awards all electors to the winning presidential candidate"(Office of Federal Register 7).
Presidential candidates may focus on high-electoral-vote states rather than campaigning nationwide(Plumer 13).
This goes against the american concept of "all men are created equal", leaving voters feeling undervauled and not important.
Second, "A tie in the nationwide electoral vote is possible because the total number of votes-538- is an even number.." (Posner 18).
A tie is considered "highly unlikely".
An election by popular vote would further reduce the likelihood of a split nation opinion.
An additional concern regarding a tie in the electoral college is the method of resolving such a deadlock.

The  tie-breaker is left to the representatives in congress, and "Because each state casts only one vote, the single representative from Wyoming...would have as much say as the 55 representatives from California..." (Plumer 12).
This fails to grant every voter an equal voice in determining the election's outcome.
All these issues, among others, collectively illustrate the true inequity of the election process.
Entering the booth next election day, dont only think about who you are voting for, but also how you are voting for them.
It makes all the difference, and, ultimately, the popular way is the best way.

original_chunks: This work presents a scalable semi-supervised node classification method for graph-structured data, named GraphHop.

The graph contains attributes
of all nodes but labels of a few nodes.
The classical label propagation (LP) method and the emerging graph convolutional network (GCN) are two widely used semi-supervised approaches to address this problem.

The LP method is not effective in
modeling node attributes and labels jointly or facing a slow convergence rate
on large-scale graphs.
GraphHop is specifically designed to overcome these limitations.
With appropriate initial label vector embeddings, each GraphHop iteration includes two steps: label aggregation and label update.

In Step 1, each node aggregates its
neighbors' label vectors obtained in the previous iteration.

In Step 2, a new
label vector is predicted for each node based on the label of the node itself
and the aggregated label information obtained in Step 1.

This iterative
procedure exploits the neighborhood information and enables GraphHop to perform
well in an extremely small label rate setting and scale well for very large
graphs.

Experimental results show that GraphHop outperforms state-of-the-art graph learning methods on a wide range of tasks (e.g., multi-label and multi-class classification on citation networks, social graphs, and commodity consumption graphs) in graphs of various sizes.
Our codes are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/TianXieUSC/GraphHop).

original_chunks:
The rapid increase in the percentage of chronic disease patients along with
the recent pandemic pose immediate threats on healthcare expenditure and
elevate causes of death.

This calls for transforming healthcare systems away
from one-on-one patient treatment into intelligent health systems, to improve
services, access and scalability, while reducing costs.

Reinforcement Learning
(RL) has advanced substantially in solving many complex problems across diverse
applications and services.
This paper comprehensively surveys recent RL models and techniques developed or applied to support Intelligent-healthcare (I-health) systems.

This
paper can guide the readers to deeply understand the state-of-the-art regarding
the use of RL in the context of I-health.

Specifically, we first overview the challenges and architecture of I-health systems and how RL can
benefit them.

We then review the background and mathematical modeling
of different RL, Deep RL (DRL), and multi-agent RL models.

After that, we
provide a deep literature review for the applications of RL in I-health
systems.
In particular, we address three major areas: edge intelligence, smart core network, and dynamic treatment regimes.
Finally, we highlight emerging challenges and future research directions for the success of RL in I-health systems, opening the door to exploring interesting unsolved problems.

original_chunks: Reliable fall detection for older adults is crucial to prevent deaths or injuries caused by falls.

Meanwhile, a vision-based
fall detection system has shown some significant results to detect falls.
Still, numerous challenges need to be resolved.

The impact of deep learning has
changed the landscape of the vision-based system, such as action recognition.
Deep learning has not been successfully used in vision-based fall detection because it needs heavy computational resources and lots of labeled training data.

This research aims to propose a vision-based fall detection system that
improves the accuracy of fall detection in some complex environments such as
the change of light condition in the room.
This study also aims to improve video frame pre-processing.

The proposed method uses Enhanced Dynamic Optical Flow, extracting time-varying information from optical flow videos with rank pooling, enabling faster fall detection and more accurate classification under varying lighting conditions.

The experimental
results showed that the classification accuracy of the fall detection improved
by around 3% and the processing time by 40 to 50ms.
The proposed system focuses on reducing fall detection time and improving classification accuracy.
It also condenses a video into a single image via a dynamic optical flow approach, improving image pre-processing performance.

original_chunks: The Marine Corps' ACV is meant to carry Marines from ship to shore and provide armored protection on land.
It may replace some or all of the decades-old AAV fleet and is ultimately expected to deliver better amphibious capability and higher water speed.
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2014 included a provision that GAO annually review and report on the ACV program until 2018.
This report updates (1) how ACV program efforts align with acquisition best practices and (2) how the ACV increments are expected to achieve amphibious capability.
To do this work, GAO reviewed program documentation and other materials for the ACV acquisition and Navy surface connector programs.
GAO identified acquisition and analysis of alternatives best practices based on its prior body of work and DOD guidance.
GAO also interviewed program and agency officials.
The U.S. Marine Corps' Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) program has used best practices in most current activities, but its faster acquisition schedule creates potential risks.

As it nears engineering and manufacturing development, the program plans to rely on mature technologies proven in their intended environment while preserving competition, a key way to get the best value for the government's investment.

Further, GAO analyzed the ACV analysis of alternatives that the Marine Corps produced for the initial portion of the ACV development, finding that overall it met best practices by, for example, ensuring that the analysis of alternatives process was impartial.

However, the Marine Corps is using an accelerated schedule with risks, including planning the preliminary design review after development begins, contrary to best practices and potentially delaying information on whether the design performs as intended.

GAO also concluded that the planned concurrency—doing development testing and production at the same time—could raise the risk of finding deficiencies after some systems are built, potentially requiring costly modifications.
Agency officials said mature technologies reduce risk and that, although some concurrency is planned, all required testing will be finished before the production decision.
While some aspects of this acquisition do suggest lower levels of risk, these deviations could potentially increase program risk.
GAO will continue to monitor this risk as the program moves forward.

The ACV program depends heavily on future plans to gradually expand amphibious capability through three planned increments—ACV 1.1, 1.2, and 2.0—but how this capability will be achieved has not yet been determined.

ACV 1.1 – Although this increment is expected to have some amphibious capability, according to program documents, it is expected to rely on surface connector craft—vessels that enable the transportation of military assets from ship to shore.
Marine Corps and U.S. Navy officials regularly coordinate ACV 1.1 plans to operate with the surface connector fleet through coordination mechanisms such as the Surface Connector Council.
ACV 1.2 – This increment is expected to have greater amphibious capability, including the ability to self-deploy from ships.

Based on demonstrations from related programs to date, program officials believe it will reach that capability, but indicated that plans for 1.2 are expected to depend on the success of ACV 1.1 development.
ACV 2.0 – This increment represents a future decision point when the Marine Corps plans to determine how to replace the Assault Amphibious Vehicle (AAV) fleet.
The Marine Corps is examining technologies that could enable high water speed, a major advance beyond the amphibious objectives set for ACV 1.1.
Therefore, how it will achieve the amphibious capability envisioned for ACV 2.0 is undetermined.

The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2014 included a provision that GAO annually review and report on the ACV program until 2018.
This report provides an update on (1) how ACV program efforts align with acquisition best practices and (2) how the ACV increments are expected to achieve amphibious capability.
To carry out this work, GAO reviewed program documentation and other relevant materials for the ACV acquisition and Navy surface connector programs.
GAO identified acquisition and analysis of alternatives best practices based on its prior body of work and DOD guidance.
GAO also interviewed program and agency officials involved in these efforts.
The U.S. Marine Corps' Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV) program has incorporated best practices in most of its current activities, but its faster acquisition schedule introduces potential risks.

As it approaches engineering and manufacturing development, the program plans to rely on mature technologies that have been proven in their intended environment while also preserving competition, which is a key means of obtaining the best value for the government's investment.

Further, GAO analyzed the ACV analysis of alternatives that the Marine Corps produced for the initial portion of the ACV development, finding that overall it met best practices by, for example, ensuring that the analysis of alternatives process was impartial.

However, the Marine Corps is following an accelerated schedule that carries risks, including planning the preliminary design review after development begins, contrary to best practices and potentially delaying insight into whether the design performs as intended.

GAO also concluded that the planned concurrency—conducting development testing and production at the same time—could increase the risk of discovering deficiencies after some systems are built, potentially leading to costly modifications.
Agency officials said that mature technologies reduce risk and that, although some concurrency is planned, all required testing will be completed before the production decision is made.
While some aspects of this acquisition do suggest lower levels of risk, these deviations could potentially increase program risk.
GAO will continue to monitor this risk as the program moves forward through later stages.

The ACV program depends heavily on future plans to incrementally expand amphibious capability through three planned increments—ACV 1.1, 1.2, and 2.0—but the way this capability will be achieved has not yet been determined.

ACV 1.1 – Although this increment is expected to have some amphibious capability, according to program documents, it is expected to rely on surface connector craft—vessels that enable the transportation of military assets from ship to shore.
Marine Corps and U.S. Navy officials regularly coordinate ACV 1.1 plans to operate with the surface connector fleet through coordination mechanisms such as the Surface Connector Council.
ACV 1.2 – This increment is expected to have greater amphibious capability, including the ability to self-deploy from ships.

Based on demonstrations from related programs to date, program officials believe it will achieve that capability, but they indicated that plans for 1.2 are expected to depend on the success of ACV 1.1 development.
ACV 2.0 – This increment represents a future decision point when the Marine Corps plans to determine how to replace the Assault Amphibious Vehicle (AAV) fleet.
The Marine Corps is examining technologies that could enable high water speed, which would represent a major advance beyond the amphibious objectives established for ACV 1.1.
Therefore, how it will achieve the amphibious capability envisioned for ACV 2.0 is undetermined.

original_chunks: The FCC is responsible for ensuring that the public knows when and by whom it is being persuaded.
Broadcasters must disclose the identity of any group or individual paying for commercial or political programming.
Political ads are regulated by the Federal Election Commission (FEC).
Recognition of sponsored programming has become increasingly difficult because of new technologies and increased access to sponsored programming such as video news releases.

GAO (1) describes requirements for sponsorship identification and federal election disclaimers and stakeholders' views of the requirements and (2) assesses how and to what extent FCC and FEC address complaints.
GAO reviewed relevant laws, guidance, and enforcement procedures, and interviewed agency officials and stakeholders about enforcement processes and actions.

Sponsorship identification statutes and regulations, overseen by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), require broadcasters to identify commercial content--usually an advertisement, an embedded advertisement, or a video news release--that has been broadcast in exchange for payment or other consideration.
A written or verbal sponsorship announcement must be made at least once during any sponsored commercial content unless the sponsor is obvious.

For content considered political or that discusses a controversial issue, broadcasters must follow all requirements for commercial content and additional requirements, such as identifying officials associated with the entity paying for an advertisement.
The FEC enforces federal election law requiring all political communications for a federal election, including television and radio advertisements, to include a disclaimer statement.
The FEC also manages requirements related to reporting campaign funding and expenditures, including funds allocated for political advertising.
The FCC provides guidance to broadcasters on when a sponsorship announcement is necessary, such as when a deejay receives payment for airing specific content.
While broadcasters find this guidance useful, it addresses older technology that is no longer used in some cases.

Furthermore, some broadcasters indicated that it would be helpful for FCC to clarify how the guidance applies in some situations, such as when a video news release or product is used during programming.

According to FCC, it opened 369 sponsorship identification cases representing just over 1 percent of the Investigations and Hearings Division's total cases opened from the beginning of 2000 through 2011.
In 22 of these cases, FCC issued enforcement actions with varying types of violations and enforcement actions.
While FCC follows standard procedures when addressing complaints, it does not inform the broadcaster named in the complaint of the outcome of the investigation in many cases.
Most broadcasters confirmed that FCC does not inform them of the status of investigations, and some indicated they currently do not know the status of several investigations.
According to FCC, it does not communicate status with broadcasters named in complaints because, among other reasons, it has no legal obligation to do so.
Broadcasters reported the lack of information about cases and FCC decisions creates uncertainty about the propriety of their past actions.
As a result, broadcasters might not have sufficient information to determine whether they should modify their practices.
This can result in stations' editing content because of unwritten regulatory policy or what they assume the policy to be.
Moreover, these investigations can be lengthy, taking from 10 months to over 5 years to complete when an enforcement action is involved.
From 2000 through May 2012, FEC opened 301 cases based on complaints alleging violations of political advertisement disclaimer requirements.
The FEC imposed civil penalties in 29 cases, 7 of which were related to television or radio advertisement disclaimers.
Unlike FCC, FEC provides status updates to those involved in investigations and issues reports explaining investigation findings.
The FEC also issues reports that explain case dismissals.
These reports can clarify acceptable and unacceptable practices for the regulated community.

original_chunks: Collaboration between the federal government and the aviation industry has led to reductions in aviation emissions, but growing air traffic has partially offset these reductions.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), working with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and others, aims to improve national airspace efficiency, safety, and capacity while reducing aviation emissions by replacing the current air traffic control system with the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen).
This effort involves new technologies and air traffic procedures that can reduce aviation emissions and incorporates research and development (R&D) on emissions-reduction technologies.

Cutting aviation emissions is vital for protecting public health and the environment and for easing concerns that could restrict airport infrastructure growth and aviation operations needed to meet demand.

This section covers (1) the scope and features of aviation emissions, (2) the current status of selected major federal actions to reduce aviation emissions, and (3) upcoming actions and obstacles to further reduce aviation emissions.
The testimony updates earlier GAO work using FAA data, literature reviews, and interviews with agency officials, industry and environmental stakeholders, and selected experts.
Aviation makes up a modest but rising share of total U.S. emissions, and these emissions harm public health and the environment.

Aircraft and airport emissions, including activity from service and passenger vehicles, produce ozone and other substances that worsen local air pollution, as well as carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that drive climate change.

EPA estimates that aviation emissions account for less than 1 percent of local air pollution nationwide and about 2.7 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, though they are projected to increase as air traffic grows.
Two key federal efforts, if implemented effectively, can help to reduce aviation emissions--NextGen initiatives in the near term and research and development over the longer term.

For example, NextGen technologies and procedures, such as satellite-based navigation systems, should allow for more direct routing, which could improve fuel efficiency and reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

Federal research and development efforts--led by FAA and NASA in collaboration with industry and academia--have achieved significant reductions in aircraft emissions through improved aircraft and engine technologies, and federal officials and aviation experts agree that such efforts are the most effective means of achieving further reductions in the longer term.
Federal R&D on aviation emissions also focuses on improving the scientific understanding of aviation emissions and developing lower-emitting aviation fuels.

Next steps in reducing aviation emissions include managing NextGen initiatives efficiently; deploying NextGen technologies and procedures as soon as practicable to realize their benefits, including lower emissions levels; and managing a decline in R&D funding, in part, by setting priorities for R&D on NextGen and emissions-reduction technologies.

Efforts to cut aviation emissions face hurdles, including designing aircraft that reduce both noise and air pollutant and greenhouse-gas emissions; persuading financially strained airlines to buy more fuel-efficient aircraft and emissions-reduction technologies; assessing how stricter EPA air quality standards and public concern about aviation emissions affect airport expansion; and addressing the impact of proposed domestic and international greenhouse gas reduction measures on the financial health and competitiveness of U.S. airlines.

Reducing aviation emissions is important both to minimize their adverse health and environmental effects and to alleviate public concerns about them that could constrain the expansion of airport infrastructure and aviation operations needed to meet demand.

This testimony addresses (1) the scope and nature of aviation emissions, (2) the status of selected key federal efforts to reduce aviation emissions, and (3) next steps and challenges in reducing aviation emissions.
The testimony updates prior GAO work with FAA data, literature reviews, and interviews with agency officials, industry and environmental stakeholders, and selected experts.
Aviation contributes a modest but growing proportion of total U.S. emissions, and these emissions contribute to adverse health and environmental effects.

Aircraft and airport operations, including those of service and passenger vehicles, emit ozone and other substances that contribute to local air pollution, as well as carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

EPA estimates that aviation emissions account for less than 1 percent of local air pollution nationwide and about 2.7 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions, but these emissions are expected to grow as air traffic increases.
Two key federal efforts, if implemented effectively, can help to reduce aviation emissions--NextGen initiatives in the near term and research and development over the longer term.

For example, NextGen technologies and procedures, such as satellite-based navigation systems, should allow for more direct routing, which could improve fuel efficiency and reduce carbon dioxide emissions.

Federal research and development efforts--led by FAA and NASA in collaboration with industry and academia--have achieved significant reductions in aircraft emissions through improved aircraft and engine technologies, and federal officials and aviation experts agree that such efforts are the most effective means of achieving further reductions in the longer term.
Federal R&D on aviation emissions also focuses on improving the scientific understanding of aviation emissions and developing lower-emitting aviation fuels.

Next steps in reducing aviation emissions include managing NextGen initiatives efficiently; deploying NextGen technologies and procedures as soon as practicable to realize their benefits, including lower emissions levels; and managing a decline in R&D funding, in part, by setting priorities for R&D on NextGen and emissions-reduction technologies.

Challenges in reducing aviation emissions include designing aircraft that can simultaneously reduce noise and emissions of air pollutants and greenhouse gases; encouraging financially stressed airlines to purchase more fuel-efficient aircraft and emissions-reduction technologies; addressing the impact on airport expansion of more stringent EPA air quality standards and growing public concerns about the effects of aviation emissions; and responding to proposed domestic and international measures for reducing greenhouse gases that could affect the financial solvency and competitiveness of U.S. airlines.

original_chunks: Deep models trained in supervised mode have achieved remarkable success across various tasks.

When labeled samples are limited, self-supervised learning
(SSL) is emerging as a new paradigm for making use of large amounts of
unlabeled samples.

SSL has achieved promising performance on natural language
and image learning tasks.
There is a growing trend to apply similar successes to graph data using graph neural networks (GNNs).
This survey provides a comprehensive overview of various approaches to training GNNs with SSL.

Specifically, we
categorize SSL methods into contrastive and predictive models.

In either
category, we provide a unified framework for methods as well as how these
methods differ in each component under the framework.

Our unified treatment of
SSL methods for GNNs sheds light on the similarities and differences of various
methods, setting the stage for developing new methods and algorithms.
We also summarize different SSL settings and the corresponding datasets used in each setting.
To support further research and comparative analysis, we create a standardized testbed for SSL in GNNs, featuring implementations of common baseline methods, datasets, and evaluation metrics.

original_chunks:
For the last ten years, CAPTCHAs have been widely used by websites to prevent
their data being automatically updated by machines.

By supposedly allowing only
humans to do so, CAPTCHAs take advantage of the reverse Turing test (TT),
knowing that humans are more intelligent than machines.
Overall, CAPTCHAs have mostly blocked machines, though this is rapidly changing as technology advances.

Hence, advanced research into optical character recognition (OCR) is overtaking
attempts to strengthen CAPTCHAs against machine-based attacks.

This paper
investigates the immunity of CAPTCHA, which was built on the failure of the TT.
We show that a simple OCR machine created for this study can easily break some CAPTCHAs.
By examining other techniques, we show that advanced OCR machines can break even more challenging CAPTCHAs.
Recent OCR advances are likely to let machines pass the TT in image recognition, the very domain where they aim to defeat CAPTCHAs.

We
improve traditional CAPTCHAs by using not only characters but also natural
language and multiple objects in the same CAPTCHA.

The proposed CAPTCHAs
might be able to hold out against machines, at least until the advent of a
machine that passes the TT completely.

original_chunks: Several vehicle manufacturers are developing or deploying automated driving systems (ADS) with freeway-pilot functionality.

This type of ADS is typically
limited to restricted-access freeways only, that is, the transition from manual
to automated modes takes place only after the ramp merging process is completed
manually.

One major challenge to extend the automation to ramp merging is that
the automated vehicle needs to incorporate and optimize long-term objectives
(e.g. successful and smooth merge) when near-term actions must be safely
executed.

Moreover, the merging process involves interactions with other
vehicles whose behaviors are sometimes hard to predict but may influence the
merging vehicle optimal actions.

To tackle such a complicated control problem,
we propose to apply Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) techniques for finding an
optimal driving policy by maximizing the long-term reward in an interactive
environment.

Specifically, we use a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) framework to model the interactive environment, producing an internal state that encodes historical driving information for a Deep Q-Network (DQN).
The DQN approximates the Q-function by using this internal state as input to output Q-values for action selection.
Under this DRL setup, prior environment interactions affecting long-term reward are remembered and used to select the best control policy.
The proposed architecture can be extended to other autonomous driving scenarios, such as navigating complex intersections or changing lanes under varying traffic conditions.

original_chunks: The Department of Labor (Labor) collects information on fees charged to 401(k) plans primarily through its Form 5500.
Labor issued final regulations in November 2007, making changes to, among other things, Schedule C of the Form 5500.
Labor emphasized reporting indirect compensation paid to and among service providers to capture all costs incurred by plan sponsors.
Congress and other stakeholders are concerned that Labor's rules may cause duplicative and confusing reporting.

Given these concerns, Government Accountability Office (GAO) was asked to examine the new requirements and assess whether they will provide (1) clear guidance to plan sponsors and (2) useful information to Labor and others.
GAO analyzed Labor's regulations and interviewed Labor and other officials about disclosure and reporting practices.
Sponsors and service providers reported confusion about Labor's new Form 5500 Schedule C reporting requirements and plan expense definitions.

Specifically, they have questions regarding the distinction between eligible and ineligible indirect compensation, that is, which types of indirect compensation must be reported on the Form 5500 (compensation that qualifies as "eligible" does not have to be reported).
To date, Labor's Web site guidance has been limited and, according to the sponsors and service providers GAO interviewed, has raised additional unanswered questions.

Specifically, Labor has not provided sufficient guidance for sponsors and providers to accurately determine what elements of compensation qualify as eligible indirect compensation (fees or expense reimbursements charged to investment funds and reflected in the value of the investment).
Therefore, interpretations have been left up to sponsors and providers and may result in a range of reporting practices, causing Labor to receive inconsistent and incomplete data.
Besides the new Form 5500 requirements, Labor has proposed but not finalized another regulation on service provider fee disclosure (its 408(b)(2) regulation).
The sponsors and service providers GAO interviewed stressed the importance of coordinating this initiative with the new Form 5500 requirements.

Such coordination could cut service providers' burden and cost of modifying data-collection and reporting systems and clarify for plan sponsors what information they need to understand and compare fees charged by different service providers.

In GAO's discussions with Labor officials, they agreed that there was a need to coordinate the two regulations, and said that although they are working to finalize the proposed 408(b)(2) regulation, it is uncertain when it will be published.

Labor officials told GAO that they do not have specific plans for using the data received as a result of the new Form 5500 requirements and will wait to see what information is reported before deciding what to do with the data.

Although Labor's new requirements are meant to ensure that plan sponsors obtain the information they need to assess the compensation paid to service providers for services rendered to the plan, the Form 5500 may not provide useful information to Labor and others.
Because plan sponsors will likely report indirect compensation in different formats, it is unclear how Labor will compare data across plans.

GAO has also previously reported that information submitted to Labor on the Form 5500 has limited value for effectively overseeing 401(k) plan fees because it does not specifically identify all fees paid from plan assets, even though those fees make up most 401(k) plan fees.

For example, plan sponsors are not required to explicitly report asset-based fees that are netted from an investment fund's performance, even though they receive this information for each of the mutual funds they offer in the 401(k) plan.
Accordingly, even with the Form 5500 changes, the newly reported information may not be very useful to Labor, plan sponsors, and others.

original_chunks: From January 2002 through November 2015, 17,911 servicemembers died while on active duty, leaving approximately 24,000 surviving dependents.
Military casualty assistance programs guide these survivors through the casualty assistance process after a servicemember's death.
Senate Report 114-49 included a provision for GAO to review the Gold Star Advocate Program and casualty assistance officer training.

This report assesses the extent to which (1) DOD and the Coast Guard have implemented the Gold Star Advocate Program and conducted outreach to survivors; and (2) DOD has developed a training program for casualty assistance officers consistent with attributes of an effective training program.
GAO analyzed statutes, DOD and Coast Guard policies on casualty matters, and DOD's military services' casualty assistance guidance and training materials.
GAO interviewed officials involved in the Gold Star Advocate Program at DOD, its military services, and the Coast Guard—which is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

DOD and the Coast Guard began the Gold Star Advocate Program in 2014, designating advocates who address, resolve, and report survivor concerns, and engaging in some outreach; however, formal management policies are not yet established.
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2014 mandated appointing personnel to support families of servicemembers who died on active duty.
Known as Gold Star Advocates, these personnel are available at any point in the casualty assistance process.
Survivors can contact a Gold Star Advocate if dissatisfied with casualty assistance.

According to DOD officials, few issues have risen to the level of the program's attention because survivor issues are generally resolved by casualty assistance officers—who serve as liaison between the survivor and the service branch following the death of a servicemember, and assist with funeral arrangements and the application and receipt of benefits and entitlements—and long-term assistance programs, which are available to provide support throughout a survivor's lifetime.
Despite implementation, neither DOD nor the Coast Guard has established governing policies, including defined roles, responsibilities, or operational protocols.

Additionally, although DOD and the Coast Guard have conducted some outreach for the program, they have not developed goals and metrics for outreach, without which some survivors may remain unaware of the casualty assistance available to them.
While designed for all survivors of servicemembers who died on active duty, the program's outreach mainly targets those whose loved ones passed away since its 2014 inception.

DOD and its military services have developed a casualty assistance officer training program that addresses the duties required of casualty assistance officers that is consistent with some attributes of an effective training program, but DOD and its military services may not have the indicators needed to evaluate the effect of that training on casualty assistance program performance.
For instance, DOD's web-based survey on casualty assistance quality has only about a 10 percent response rate.
With such a low response rate, DOD acknowledged that results should be interpreted cautiously.
Without better indicators for evaluating casualty assistance officer training, DOD may lack information to improve survivor assistance quality.

original_chunks: TSA acquisition programs add billions to life cycle costs and support aviation security initiatives, including passenger and baggage screening technologies.
Within DHS, TSA is responsible for establishing requirements for testing and deploying transportation system technologies.
GAO has noted since 2010 that DHS and TSA faced challenges in managing acquisition efforts, including deploying untested and unmet requirements technologies.

This testimony addresses (1) TSA's handling of challenges in developing and meeting program requirements, testing new screening technologies, and delivering capabilities within cost and schedule estimates for selected programs, and (2) DHS efforts to strengthen oversight of component acquisition processes.

This testimony is based on GAO products from January 2010 through January 2013, including updates in March 2013 on TSA's implementation of GAO's prior recommendations and preliminary observations from ongoing work.
GAO conducted updates and ongoing work by reviewing documents like the AIT road map and interviewing TSA officials.
TSA has taken steps to address challenges in developing, testing, and delivering screening technologies for selected aviation security programs, but challenges remain.
In January 2012, GAO reported TSA faced difficulties in developing and meeting key performance requirements for advanced imaging technology (AIT) acquisition.

Specifically, GAO found that TSA did not fully follow Department of Homeland Security (DHS) acquisition policies when acquiring AIT, which resulted in DHS approving nationwide AIT deployment without full knowledge of TSA's revised specifications.
DHS required TSA to notify DHS's Acquisition Review Board (ARB) if AIT could not meet any of TSA's five key performance parameters or if TSA changed a key performance parameter during testing.
However, GAO found that the ARB approved TSA for full-scale production without reviewing the changed parameter.
DHS officials stated the ARB should have formally reviewed this change to ensure TSA did not change it arbitrarily.
GAO recommended that TSA develop a road map that outlines vendors' progress in meeting all key performance parameters.
DHS agreed, and developed a road map to address the recommendation, but faces challenges implementing it--e.g., due to vendor delays.
Additionally, in January 2013, GAO reported that TSA faced challenges related to testing and deploying passenger screening canine teams.
GAO concluded TSA began deploying canine teams to airport terminals in April 2011 before determining their operational effectiveness.
In June 2012, DHS and TSA started operational assessments to demonstrate canine teams' effectiveness.
Also, TSA began deploying teams before it had completed an assessment to determine where within the airport the canine teams would be most effectively utilized.
GAO recommended that on the basis of DHS assessment results, TSA expand and complete testing to assess the effectiveness of canine teams in areas of the airport deemed appropriate.

DHS agreed and officials stated that as of April 2013, TSA had completed testing in collaboration with DHS of canine teams in airport sterile areas and is conducting tests on its own in airport sterile and public areas.
DHS has some efforts under way to strengthen its oversight of component investment and acquisition processes, but additional actions are needed.

In September 2012, GAO reported that while DHS had initiated efforts to address the department's acquisition management challenges, most of DHS's major acquisition programs continue to cost more than expected, take longer to deploy than planned, or deliver less capability than promised.

GAO identified 42 DHS programs that experienced cost growth, schedule slips, or both, with 16 of the programs' costs increasing from a total of $19.7 billion in 2008 to $52.2 billion in 2011--an aggregate increase of 166 percent.
GAO concluded DHS recognized the need to implement its acquisition policy more consistently, but significant work remained.
GAO suggested DHS revise acquisition policy to better incorporate key program and portfolio management practices and ensure full compliance with DHS acquisition policy.
DHS agreed, and in September 2012 officials stated that it was in the process of revising its policy to more fully reflect key program management practices.

original_chunks: Five years after playing in the seventh tier, Jamie Vardy was making his England debut, breaking records and on the way to winning the Premier League title.
Now, thanks to over £100,000 of the Leicester City striker's own money, Newport County hope they have found a star who can follow his remarkable rise to the top.
In June, Lamar Reynolds was among 42 non-league players at the Jamie Vardy V9 Academy, training and living for a week at Manchester City's complex under scouts from more than 65 professional clubs.
The 21-year-old is one of three graduates to sign with Football League clubs so far and has already impressed in the Exiles' pre-season campaign. "
I like to get goals," says Reynolds, who last year bagged 27 in 36 games for Brentwood Town in the Isthmian League Division One North, tier eight of the English football pyramid. "
I just want to quickly make an impact and show that there's talent in the non-league which is where I came from, that's the main target for me."
With transfer fees and wages at the top soaring, the V9 Academy's main aim is to show clubs that hidden gems can still be found lower down the football pyramid if they look carefully enough.

After Sheffield Wednesday released him at 16, Vardy worked in a carbon-fibre splint factory before playing for Stocksbridge Park Steels, FC Halifax and Fleetwood, from where Leicester signed him for £1m. At the age of 25, Vardy was only earning £850 a week; within three years he would set a new Premier League record by scoring in 11 consecutive matches.
His 2016 autobiography, 'From Nowhere', aptly captures that extraordinary period. "
He's been a big idol for a lot of players in non-league," adds Reynolds. "
We saw him twice in the week I think.
We had a couple of Q&A sessions with him and heard about his time in non-league.
I learned a lot from what he said, so the experience was entirely positive.
His main message was never give up.
He told us it can be hard to stay focused and keep your head, but you have to know your target, work hard and never give up. "
I've taken that advice on board, and things are obviously going well for me so far.
I think it has helped me a lot because I was with many players who have been in and out of the [Football] League before and are quality players."
It may be too early to draw too many comparisons between the Leicester striker and any of his academy graduates, but Vardy has shown that anything is possible.

Reynolds is understood to have been one of the standout players from the V9 class of 2017 and has already drawn attention in Newport's amber and black by scoring in a friendly win at Swindon Supermarine. "
I am confident I can score as many goals as last season.
That's the main target anyway," he says. "
Fingers crossed and, as long as I work hard, I'll definitely be able to get it. "
There were a few other offers but I looked here and saw that I could relate to a few things here so I thought this would be the best place for me to go. "
After they showed that much faith in me [with a two-year deal] it was a no-brainer for me really.
Whenever I am on the pitch, I want to work hard and repay the manager's faith in me.
If he goes on to achieve half as much as his mentor Vardy has done, Newport will consider that two-year contract a sound investment.

original_chunks: Terrorist and criminal watch list systems--sometimes referred to as watchout, lookout, target, or tip-off systems--are important tools in controlling and protecting our nation's borders.
The events of September 11, 2001, and other incidents since then, have highlighted the need to share these watch lists.

In light of the importance of border security, GAO was asked to identify federal databases and systems that contain watch lists, the agencies that maintain and use them in protecting our nation's borders, the kind of data they contain, whether federal agencies are sharing information from these lists with each other and with state and local governments and private organizations, the structural characteristics of those lists that are automated, and whether opportunities exist to consolidate these watch lists.

Overall, the federal government manages watch list use for border security in a decentralized, uneven way, largely because each list was created to fit a particular agency's distinct mission, legal requirements, culture, and systems context.

Specifically, nine federal agencies--which prior to the creation of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spanned the Departments of Defense, Justice, State, Transportation, and the Treasury--develop and maintain 12 watch lists.
These lists include overlapping but not identical sets of data, and different policies and procedures govern whether and how these data are shared with others.
Generally, sharing is more common among federal agencies than between federal agencies and either state and local government agencies or private organizations.
In addition, electronic data sharing is constrained by key differences in the watch lists' systems architecture, such as hardware, software, networks, and data characteristics.
Two agencies also pointed to possible ways to standardize and merge the lists, which GAO believes would enhance information sharing.
The President's homeland security strategy further recognizes the need to address the proliferation of these lists.

Although the Office of Homeland Security reportedly sought consolidation for an enterprise architecture border and transportation security blueprint, the DHS Chief Information Officer told us the department had recently assumed responsibility for the blueprint.
However, we lacked enough information to evaluate those efforts.

original_chunks:
Three-dimensional objects are commonly represented as 3D boxes in a
point-cloud.
This approach mimics well-researched image-based 2D bounding-box detection, but adds difficulties.
Since 3D objects lack static orientation, box-based methods struggle to accommodate all angles or precisely enclose rotated objects with axis-aligned bounding boxes.
Here, we propose representing, detecting, and tracking 3D objects as points instead.

Our framework, CenterPoint, first detects
centers of objects using a keypoint detector and regresses to other attributes,
including 3D size, 3D orientation, and velocity.

In a second stage, it refines
these estimates using additional point features on the object.
CenterPoint tracks 3D objects using a greedy closest-point matching strategy.
The resulting detection and tracking algorithm is simple, efficient, and effective.

CenterPoint achieved state-of-the-art performance on the nuScenes benchmark for
both 3D detection and tracking, with 65.5 NDS and 63.8 AMOTA for a single
model.

On the Waymo Open Dataset, CenterPoint outperforms all previous single
model method by a large margin and ranks first among all Lidar-only
submissions.
Pre-trained models and source code are available at https://github.com/tianweiy/CenterPoint.

Three-dimensional objects are commonly represented as 3D boxes in a
point-cloud.

This particular approach to object representation in 3D space closely mimics the well-researched methods of image-based 2D bounding-box detection, but inherently introduces a new set of difficulties and challenges.

Since three-dimensional objects in real-world scenarios typically lack a static orientation, traditional box-based methods often struggle significantly to accommodate all possible angles or to precisely enclose rotated objects when using conventional axis-aligned bounding boxes.

Here, in contrast to existing methodologies, we propose an innovative approach centered on representing, detecting, and tracking these three-dimensional objects as individual points rather than as volumetric boxes.

Our framework, CenterPoint, first detects
centers of objects using a keypoint detector and regresses to other attributes,
including 3D size, 3D orientation, and velocity.
In a subsequent second stage of processing, the framework further refines these initial estimates by leveraging additional point features identified on the detected object itself.
CenterPoint efficiently tracks the detected three-dimensional objects over time by employing a robust greedy closest-point matching strategy.

The resulting detection and tracking algorithm, developed through this innovative approach, is characterized by its simplicity, computational efficiency, and overall effectiveness in real-world applications.

CenterPoint achieved state-of-the-art performance on the nuScenes benchmark for
both 3D detection and tracking, with 65.5 NDS and 63.8 AMOTA for a single
model.

On the Waymo Open Dataset, CenterPoint outperforms all previous single
model method by a large margin and ranks first among all Lidar-only
submissions.
Pre-trained models and the comprehensive source code for CenterPoint are readily available for public access and further research at the provided URL: https://github.com/tianweiy/CenterPoint.

original_chunks: The HBO fantasy drama won three awards Sunday, including outstanding drama series.
The show's total number of awards now stands at 38, which means it has beaten Frasier's previous record of 37.
British winners included Dame Maggie Smith, who won outstanding supporting actress in a drama series for Downton Abbey.
It's Dame Maggie's third Emmy for playing Violet Crawley, but she has never attended.
Host Jimmy Kimmel joked: "We're not mailing this to her.
Dame Maggie, if you want this award, it will be in lost and found.
BBC One's Sherlock special, "The Abominable Bride," was named best made-for-TV movie.
Accepting the award, Sherlock creator Steven Moffatt made reference to the The Great British Bake off, currently shown on BBC One but bought by Channel 4 last week.
He said: "Thank you to the BBC who we love above all bakery.
That statement will resonate with British audiences.
Susanne Bier, the Danish director of the BBC's spy thriller The Night Manager, won for best directing in a limited series.

Bier, who was the only female nominee in the category, told BBC Breakfast: "This is such a traditional men's world, and I hope the fact a woman director has won this prestigious prize is going to mean that more non-conventional series and movies are going to be directed by women."
John Oliver won best variety talk series for his HBO series Last Week Tonight, beating fellow British nominee James Corden, who was nominated for The Late Late Show.
For the second year, Veep won outstanding comedy series, and Julia Louis-Dreyfus earned her fifth award for outstanding lead comedy actress.
In her acceptance speech, Louis-Dreyfus said: "Our show started out as political satire but now feels like a sobering documentary."
She dedicated her award to her father, who died on Friday.
The outstanding comedy actor gong went to Jeffrey Tambor, who plays a transgender woman in the Amazon series Transparent, for the second year in a row.
Accepting the award, Tambor encouraged the industry to offer more opportunities to the trans community. "
I would not be unhappy were I the last cisgender male to play a transgender female on television.
Much progress remains to be made," he asserted.
Rami Malek won outstanding lead actor in a drama series for his role in Mr Robot - the first time an actor from an ethnic minority has won the award since 1998.
Tatiana Maslany won outstanding lead actress in a drama series for her performance in Orphan Black.
The People v. O.J. The show won five trophies including outstanding limited series plus acting gongs for Sarah Paulson, Sterling K Brown and Courtney B Vance.
Kate McKinnon, from the all-female Ghostbusters reboot, won outstanding supporting actress in a comedy series for Saturday Night Live.
The Netflix series Master of None won its first Emmy for outstanding writing for a comedy series.
The show's co-writer Alan Yang called for better Asian representation on screen in his acceptance speech.
Additionally, The Voice won outstanding reality competition series, beating Project Runway and Dancing With The Stars.
Game of Thrones' 38 Emmy Awards include nine trophies from the Creative Arts Emmys last weekend.
While HBO's Game of Thrones is the most awarded drama series in Emmy history, Saturday Night Live holds the overall record with 44 wins.
Kimmel made several references to diversity during the ceremony in light of the "Oscars So White" controversy earlier this year.
In his opening monologue, he joked, "Here in Hollywood, the only thing we value more than diversity is congratulating ourselves on how much we value diversity." "

model is provided with a text description and an outline of the type of face,

generating better images.

original_chunks: Assessing time-series predictability and complexity is fundamental for designing and controlling nonlinear systems.
Many entropy-based measures have been proposed to evaluate time-series predictability and complexity.

However, the existed methods have some drawbacks related to a
strong dependence of entropy on the parameters of the methods, as well as on
the length and amplitude of the time series.

To overcome these difficulties,
this study proposes a new method for estimating the entropy of a time series
using the LogNNet neural network model.
According to our algorithm, the LogNNet reservoir matrix is filled with time-series elements.
The network is trained on the MNIST-10 dataset, then its classification accuracy is calculated.

The
accuracy is considered as the entropy measure and denoted by NNetEn.

The
novelty of entropy calculation is that the time series is involved in mixing
the input information in the reservoir.

The greater complexity of the time
series leads to the better ability of the neural network to learn, and to the
higher classification accuracy and NNetEn values.
The number of LogNNet training epochs is used as the control parameter.
We introduce a new time-series characteristic, termed time series learning inertia, that characterizes the neural network's learning rate.

The method's
robustness and efficiency are verified on chaotic, periodic,
random, binary and constant time series.

The comparison of NNetEn with other
methods of entropy estimation demonstrates that our method is more robust and
accurate and can be widely used in practice.

original_chunks: We present a VSM-based algorithm for learning from unlabeled text that solves SAT verbal analogy questions.

A verbal analogy
has the form A:B::C:D, meaning "A is to B as C is to D"; for example,
mason:stone::carpenter:wood.

SAT analogy questions provide a word pair, A:B,
and the problem is to select the most analogous word pair, C:D, from a set of
five choices.

The VSM algorithm correctly answers 47% of a collection of 374
college-level analogy questions (random guessing would yield 20% correct; the
average college-bound senior high school student answers about 57% correctly).
We motivate the study by applying it to a difficult NLP task: identifying semantic relations in noun-modifier pairs.
For each noun-modifier pair, such as "laser printer", we assign a semantic-relation label capturing the relation between the noun (printer) and modifier (laser).

We use a supervised nearest-neighbour algorithm that assigns a class to a given
noun-modifier pair by finding the most analogous noun-modifier pair in the
training data.

With 30 classes of semantic relations, on a collection of 600
labeled noun-modifier pairs, the learning algorithm attains an F value of 26.5%
(random guessing: 3.3%).
With only 5 semantic-relation classes, the F value rises to 43.2% (random: 20%).
The method achieves state-of-the-art results for both verbal analogies and noun-modifier relations.

original_chunks: Efforts to combat terrorism have become an increasingly important part of government activities.
These efforts have also become important in the United States' relations with other countries and with international organizations, such as the United Nations (U.N.).
The Department of State oversees these initiatives and protects Americans abroad.

State has helped direct the U.S. efforts to combat terrorism abroad by building the global coalition against terrorism, including providing diplomatic support for military operations in Afghanistan and other countries.

State has also supported international law enforcement efforts to identify, arrest, and bring terrorists to justice, as well as performing other activities intended to reduce the number of terrorist attacks.
The State Department conducts multifaceted activities in its effort to prevent terrorist attacks on Americans abroad.
For Americans traveling or living abroad, State issues public travel warnings and maintains systems to communicate terrorism-related information.
For American businesses and universities overseas, State uses the Overseas Security Advisory Councils--voluntary State-private sector partnerships--to exchange threat information.
To disrupt and destroy terrorist organizations abroad, State has numerous programs and activities that rely on military, multilateral, economic, law enforcement, intelligence, and other capabilities.

State uses extradition treaties to bring terrorists to trial in the United States and cooperates with foreign intelligence, security, and law enforcement entities to track and capture terrorists in foreign countries.
When the United States lacks extradition agreements with a country, State, with the Department of Justice, may seek suspected terrorists' arrest overseas through renditions.
The State Department leads the U.S. response to terrorist incidents abroad.
This includes diplomatic measures to protect Americans, minimize harm, prevent attacks, and bring terrorists to justice.

To coordinate the U.S. international counterterrorism effort, State uses various mechanisms to work with the Departments of Defense, Justice, and the Treasury; the intelligence agencies; the Federal Bureau of Investigation; and others.
These include headquarters-level interagency working groups in Washington, D.C., emergency action committees at U.S. missions overseas, and liaison exchanges with other government agencies.

The Department of State oversees these initiatives and works to protect Americans abroad through these efforts.

State has helped direct the U.S. efforts to combat terrorism abroad by building the global coalition against terrorism, including providing diplomatic support for military operations in Afghanistan and other countries.

State has also supported international law enforcement efforts to identify, arrest, and bring terrorists to justice, as well as performing other activities intended to reduce the number of terrorist attacks.
The State Department conducts multifaceted activities in its effort to prevent terrorist attacks on Americans abroad.
For Americans traveling or living abroad, State issues public travel warnings and maintains systems to communicate information related to terrorism.
For American businesses and universities overseas, State uses the Overseas Security Advisory Councils--voluntary State-private sector partnerships--to exchange information about threats.
To disrupt and destroy terrorist organizations abroad, State has numerous programs and activities that rely on military, multilateral, economic, law enforcement, intelligence, and other capabilities.

State uses extradition treaties to bring terrorists to trial in the United States and also cooperates with foreign intelligence, security, and law enforcement entities to track and capture terrorists in foreign countries.
When the United States lacks extradition agreements with a country, State, working with the Department of Justice, may seek the overseas arrest of suspected terrorists through renditions.
The State Department leads and coordinates the U.S. response to terrorist incidents abroad.
This response includes diplomatic measures intended to protect Americans, minimize harm, prevent attacks, and bring terrorists to justice.

To coordinate the U.S. international counterterrorism effort, State uses various mechanisms to work with the Departments of Defense, Justice, and the Treasury; the intelligence agencies; the Federal Bureau of Investigation; and other relevant entities.

These mechanisms include headquarters-level interagency working groups in Washington, D.C., emergency action committees at U.S. missions overseas, and liaison exchanges with other government agencies.

original_chunks: The Marine Corps' ACV is designed to transport Marines from ship to shore and provide armored protection on land.
It aims to replace all or part of the decades-old AAV fleet and is expected to deliver enhanced amphibious capabilities and higher water speed.
The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2014 included a provision that GAO annually review and report on the ACV program until 2018.
This report examines (1) how the ACV program's initiatives align with acquisition best practices and (2) how the ACV increments will achieve amphibious capability.
GAO reviewed program documentation and other materials for the ACV acquisition and Navy surface connector programs.
GAO identified acquisition and analysis of alternatives best practices based on its prior body of work and DOD guidance.
GAO also interviewed program and agency officials.
Many current ACV program activities demonstrate the application of best practices, but the planned accelerated acquisition timeline may introduce potential risks.

As the program moves toward engineering and manufacturing development, it aims to leverage proven technologies validated in their intended environment and foster competition to maximize government investment returns.

Further, GAO analyzed the ACV analysis of alternatives that the Marine Corps produced for the initial portion of the ACV development, finding that overall it met best practices by, for example, ensuring that the analysis of alternatives process was impartial.

However, the Marine Corps is pursuing an accelerated program schedule that presents some risks, including plans to hold the preliminary design review after the start of development—a deviation from best practices which could delay the attainment of information about whether the design performs as expected.

Additionally, GAO believes the extent of planned concurrency—conducting development testing and production simultaneously—could increase the risk of identifying deficiencies after some systems have already been built, potentially leading to costly modifications.
Agency officials stated that mature technologies help reduce risk and that, although some concurrency is planned, all necessary testing will be completed before the production decision.
While some aspects of this acquisition do suggest lower levels of risk, these deviations could potentially increase program risk.
GAO will continue to monitor this risk as the program moves forward.

Marine Corps and U.S. Navy officials regularly coordinate ACV 1.1 plans to operate with the surface connector fleet through coordination mechanisms such as the Surface Connector Council.
ACV 1.2 – This increment is expected to have greater amphibious capability, including the ability to self-deploy from ships.

Based on demonstrations from related programs to date, program officials believe it will reach that capability, but indicated that plans for 1.2 are expected to depend on the success of ACV 1.1 development.
ACV 2.0 – This increment represents a future decision point when the Marine Corps plans to determine how to replace the Assault Amphibious Vehicle (AAV) fleet.
The Marine Corps is currently exploring technologies that could enable high water speed—a significant increase from the amphibious goals set for ACV 1.1.
Therefore, how it will achieve the amphibious capability envisioned for ACV 2.0 is undetermined.

Mr Huseynov, the founder of the Institute for Reporters' Freedom and Safety (IRFS), a non-governmental organisation monitoring rights violations against journalists, is accused by the Azeri government of tax evasion and abuse of power.
Authorities have brought similar charges against several other civil society activists, which rights groups call "bogus".
Like most pro-democracy NGOs, Mr Huseynov's IRFS was under surveillance by the Azeri security services.

Activists like Mr Huseynov and others currently in detention - such as Rasul Jafarov, human rights lawyer Intigam Aliyev, Leyla and Arif Yunus, and Anar Mammadli - have for years openly criticised their government, raising awareness of human rights abuses in the oil and gas-rich country.
The international community has recognised their work.
However, Azeri officials, including President Ilham Aliyev's chief adviser Ramiz Mehdiyev, have called them "traitors".
The latest target of the government's campaign to silence critics is investigative reporter Khadija Ismaylova, known for exposing corruption involving Azerbaijan's president and his family.
In December 2014, she was charged with inciting a man to commit suicide.
Last week, she was also charged with embezzlement, tax evasion and abuse of power.
Her colleagues, whom I met in December in Baku, described her detention as an attempt to silence her. "

By arresting Khadija, the government is sending a message to journalists and to the public in general that those who fight for truth and free speech, those who fight for their rights, will be arrested."
said Kamran Mahmudov, who briefly filled in for Ms Ismaylova on her popular radio talk-show on US-funded Radio Liberty.
Weeks later, the authorities raided Radio Liberty's offices and took it off the air.
Police took Kamran Mahmudov from his home in his pyjamas for questioning.
The closure of one of the few remaining independent voices in Azeri media was criticised by the US State Department, the EU and several human rights organisations.
According to the New-York based Committee to Protect Journalists, Azerbaijan is the leading jailer of journalists in Europe and Central Asia.
However, the government insists that all the charges against journalists and civil society activists are legitimate. "
No one is prosecuted in Azerbaijan based on his or her professional activities or political beliefs," said Hikmat Hajiyev, a spokesman for Azerbaijan's foreign affairs ministry. "
Khadija Ismaylova has been engaged in journalistic activities for more than 10 years and could write different stories.
There is now a real criminal case under Azerbaijan's criminal code," he added. "

They face long prison terms if found guilty of their charges.

The Kurdakhany detention facility on Baku's outskirts, where he is held, has been dubbed "the university" because many of the brightest minds seen as threats to the state are detained there.

original_chunks: A small federal agency, NMB facilitates labor relations in railroads and airlines through mediation and arbitration of labor disputes and by overseeing union elections.
Established under the Railway Labor Act, NMB's primary responsibility is to prevent work stoppages in these critical industries.
The FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012 required GAO to evaluate NMB programs and activities.
GAO reviewed NMB’s (1) strategic planning and performance measurement methods; (2) protections for major management areas; and (3) barriers it faced in overseeing elections.

GAO evaluated NMB’s management practices against internal control standards and other GAO requirements, consulted NMB officials, current and former board members, and rail and air labor and management stakeholders, and reviewed relevant federal statutes, regulations, and NMB policies.
The National Mediation Board (NMB) recently updated its strategic plan but is not meeting some federal strategic planning and performance measurement requirements.
NMB missed the deadline to update its strategic plan and lacks performance metrics to track progress toward its goals.

NMB also lacks some controls in key management areas that could risk its resources and its success: Financial accountability: NMB contracts for annual financial statement audits and internal control reviews.
However, it lacks a formal process for addressing identified deficiencies, a key internal control.

Information technology: NMB has implemented new information technology systems but still lacks key management and security controls, including an information security program that fully meets federal requirements.
Human capital: NMB has begun strengthening its human capital program, but more improvements are needed.
Although all NMB senior managers are eligible for retirement, NMB has not done formal workforce planning to identify staffing–skill gaps and approaches to address them, including training.
Procurement: NMB has put in place some procurement policies and controls, but weaknesses persist.
For example, during a recent procurement of tablet computers for select staff, NMB did not follow its procedures for determining the need or solicit competition.
Other management issues: NMB has no Inspector General (IG), and oversight by other federal agencies is limited.
NMB also has a significant number of pending rail arbitration cases, and it lacks complete data on the types of cases filed to help it address the backlog and the costs.
NMB has adapted to challenges presented by large union elections resulting from airline mergers and has implemented improvements such as online voting.
In 2010, NMB changed its rules for determining a majority in union elections.

While this process caused disagreement among some stakeholders, NMB data suggest that the percentage of elections in which a union was certified has, thus far, remained relatively constant in the years before and after the rule change.

In this paper, we propose a novel object detection framework named "Deep
Regionlets" by establishing a bridge between deep neural networks and
conventional detection schema for accurate generic object detection.
Inspired by their ability to model object deformation and various aspect ratios, we integrate regionlets into an end-to-end trainable deep learning framework.

The deep regionlets framework consists of a region
selection network and a deep regionlet learning module.

Specifically, given a
detection bounding box proposal, the region selection network provides guidance
on where to select regions to learn the features from.
The regionlet learning module selects and transforms local features to mitigate local variations.
To this end, we first implement non-rectangular region selection within the detection framework to accommodate object appearance variations.
Furthermore, we integrate a "gating network" within the regionlet learning module for soft selection and pooling of regionlets.

The Deep Regionlets framework is
trained end-to-end without additional efforts.

We perform ablation studies and
conduct extensive experiments on the PASCAL VOC and Microsoft COCO datasets.
The framework surpasses state-of-the-art algorithms like RetinaNet and Mask R-CNN, even without supplementary segmentation labels.

Axis-aligned decision forests have long been the leading class of machine
learning algorithms for modeling tabular data.
Machine learning applications like learning-to-rank benefit greatly from decision forests' performance.
They also offer advantages such as interpretability.

Despite their widespread use and rich history, decision
forests to date fail to consume raw structured data such as text, or learn
effective representations for them, a factor behind the success of deep neural
networks in recent years.

While there exist methods that construct smoothed
decision forests to achieve representation learning, the resulting models are
decision forests in name only: They are no longer axis-aligned, use stochastic
decisions, or are not interpretable.

Furthermore, none of the existing methods
are appropriate for problems that require a Transfer Learning treatment.
We propose a novel approach to enable representation learning for decision forests without new constraints or structural changes.
Our model is a decision forest, trained with any forest learning algorithm, built on a deep neural network.
By approximating decision forest gradients via input perturbation, the neural network learns or refines representations.
Our framework applies to any decision forest and allows any deep neural network for representation learning.

We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of our proposal through
experiments on synthetic and benchmark classification datasets.

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) considers settings in which a set
of coexisting agents interact with one another and their environment.
The environment becomes non-stationary as agents adapt and learn.
This poses a major challenge for value function-based algorithms, whose convergence generally assumes a stationary environment.
Policy search algorithms also struggle in multi-agent settings, as partial observability from unknown opponent actions introduces high variance into training.

Modelling an agent's opponent(s)
is often pursued as a means of resolving the issues arising from the
coexistence of learning opponents.

An opponent model provides an agent with
some ability to reason about other agents to aid its own decision making.

Most
prior works learn an opponent model by assuming the opponent is employing a
stationary policy or switching between a set of stationary policies.
Such approaches can reduce training-signal variance for policy search algorithms.

However, in the multi-agent setting, agents have an incentive to
continually adapt and learn.
This makes assumptions of opponent stationarity unrealistic.
In this work, we introduce Learning to Model Opponent Learning (LeMOL), a novel method for modelling an opponent's learning dynamics.

We show our structured opponent model is more
accurate and stable than naive behaviour cloning baselines.
We further show that opponent modelling can improve algorithmic agent performance in multi-agent settings.

original_chunks: In June 2007, SBA established the Patriot Express Pilot Loan Program within its 7(a) loan guarantee program to provide small businesses owned and operated by veterans and other eligible members of the military community access to capital.
Through Patriot Express, SBA guarantees individual small business loans that lenders originate.
GAO was asked to evaluate the program.

This report examines (1) trends in the volume and performance of Patriot Express and related SBA loan programs; (2) the effect of the program on eligible members of the military community; and (3) SBA internal controls to ensure that only eligible borrowers participate.

GAO analyzed 2007-2012 data on the performance and costs of Patriot Express and comparable SBA loan programs, interviewed selected borrowers, lenders, and veteran service organizations, and reviewed SBA guidance on borrower eligibility controls.
Patriot Express loans totaled about $703 million, had a higher default rate than SBA's other related loan guarantee programs, and generated losses exceeding income.
Except for 2007 approvals, Patriot Express loans defaulted at a higher rate than loans under SBA's primary 7(a) or streamlined SBA Express programs.
The Patriot Express program's overall default rate was significantly higher for smaller loans, especially for loans below $25,000 (20 percent).
Additionally, one lender accounted for more than 64 percent of these smaller loans and experienced higher default rates than the remaining lenders.
From 2007 to 2012, Patriot Express losses exceeded income by $31.1 million, excluding future fee revenues and recoveries from defaulted loans.

Borrowers, lenders, and veteran service organizations GAO interviewed identified benefits and challenges of Patriot Express, but SBA has not evaluated this pilot program's effect on eligible members of the military community.
Borrowers and lenders said that some benefits of the program were that it helped veterans expand their businesses and allowed them to take advantage of the streamlined application process.
Some challenges they identified were low awareness of the program and which lenders participated in the program.
In 2010, SBA extended the Patriot Express pilot through 2013 to allow time to evaluate its effect.
To date, SBA has not evaluated the program or established a plan of what it intends to do to evaluate it.
SBA officials told us that they focused their resources on evaluating 7(a) loans because there are many more of them and, therefore, they pose a greater risk to SBA than Patriot Express loans.
In addition to Patriot Express, SBA previously introduced other pilot programs that also have not been evaluated.
GAO found that program evaluation lets an agency refine design, assess whether operations produced desired benefits, and, for pilots, decide whether to make programs permanent.

Without conducting evaluations of pilot programs, SBA lacks the information needed to assess their performance and their effects on eligible participants and decide whether to extend these programs, including Patriot Express.
SBA's internal controls over lenders may not reasonably ensure that Patriot Express loans go only to eligible members of the military community and that only they benefit from the proceeds.
SBA relies on lenders to verify and document borrower eligibility when approving a loan.
One SBA control for overseeing lenders' compliance with eligibility requirements is sampling loan files during 7(a) program examinations, but few Patriot Express loans are reviewed.
Patriot Express is intended to assist only eligible members of the military community and SBA officials told us that they expect borrowers to maintain eligibility after the loan is disbursed.
However, SBA has not established procedures for lenders to reasonably ensure borrowers remain compliant with this eligibility requirement.
Federal internal control standards and GAO's fraud-prevention framework identify continuous monitoring as a key element of an effective internal control system.
Without enhanced internal controls, particularly with respect to monitoring of borrowers, SBA lacks assurance that Patriot Express loans are serving only eligible borrowers.
