original_chunks: The Department of Labor (Labor) collects information on fees charged to 401(k) plans primarily through its Form 5500.
Labor issued final regulations in November 2007, making changes to, among other things, Schedule C of the Form 5500.
Labor focused on mandatory reporting of indirect compensation among service providers to capture all costs borne by plan sponsors.
Congress and other stakeholders have raised concerns that Labor's regulations may lead to redundant and confusing reporting.
Due to these concerns, GAO was asked to examine Labor's new requirements and determine if they will provide (1) clear guidance to plan sponsors and (2) useful information to Labor and others.
GAO analyzed Labor's regulations and interviewed Labor and other officials about disclosure and reporting practices.
Plan sponsors and service providers are uncertain about Labor's revised Form 5500 Schedule C reporting mandates and the precise definition of plan expenses.

Specifically, they have questions regarding the distinction between eligible and ineligible indirect compensation, that is, which types of indirect compensation must be reported on the Form 5500 (compensation that qualifies as "eligible" does not have to be reported).
Labor's minimal online guidance has generated further unresolved inquiries, according to sponsors and service providers interviewed by GAO.

Specifically, Labor has not provided sufficient guidance for sponsors and providers to accurately determine what elements of compensation qualify as eligible indirect compensation (fees or expense reimbursements charged to investment funds and reflected in the value of the investment).
Therefore, interpretations have been left up to sponsors and providers and may result in a range of reporting practices, causing Labor to receive inconsistent and incomplete data.
In addition to new Form 5500 requirements, Labor proposed another unfinalized regulation on service provider fee disclosure (its 408(b)(2) regulation).
Sponsors and service providers GAO communicated with stressed the critical need to harmonize this initiative with the revised Form 5500 requirements.
This alignment can reduce the burden and expense for service providers in adapting data collection and reporting, and clarify essential fee information for plan sponsors to understand and compare.

In GAO's discussions with Labor officials, they agreed that there was a need to coordinate the two regulations, and said that although they are working to finalize the proposed 408(b)(2) regulation, it is uncertain when it will be published.

Labor officials told GAO that they do not have specific plans for using the data received as a result of the new Form 5500 requirements and will wait to see what information is reported before deciding what to do with the data.

Although Labor's new requirements are meant to ensure that plan sponsors obtain the information they need to assess the compensation paid to service providers for services rendered to the plan, the Form 5500 may not provide useful information to Labor and others.
Given the likely diverse reporting formats for indirect compensation, it is unclear how Labor will effectively compare data across plans.

Moreover, GAO previously observed that Form 5500 data has limited utility for overseeing 401(k) plan fees, as it doesn't explicitly detail all fees disbursed from plan assets, despite these being most 401(k) plan costs.

For example, plan sponsors are not required to explicitly report asset-based fees that are netted from an investment fund's performance, even though they receive this information for each of the mutual funds they offer in the 401(k) plan.
Consequently, despite Form 5500 revisions, the updated information may not significantly benefit Labor, plan sponsors, or other interested parties.

These contractors perform functions such as screening and enrolling providers, detecting and investigating potential fraud, and identifying improper payments and vulnerabilities that could lead to payment errors.

original_chunks: Many Ukrainians begin and end their summer holiday in Russian-annexed Crimea this way.
Queues of cars snake for several hours as people wait to visit relatives or get to the peninsula for a beach break.
As people wait to be checked or waved through in Kherson, beside Crimea where Kiev's vast Dnipro river enters the Black Sea, lorry-loads of watermelons are sold by the roadside.
Aside from the occasional roadside soldier and alert Ukraine border guards, little suggests the country is preparing for Russian military action from the south.
Most analysts think any such action would be highly unlikely.
But since Russia seized Crimea in March 2014 without a shot being fired, Ukraine has learned to expect unexpected moves from its powerful neighbour.
Vigilance is the watchword of Ukraine's National Border Guard.
Spokesman Ivan Shevcov said his colleagues were "prepared for any kind of action from the Russian side".
The war of words between Russia and Ukraine has intensified following Moscow's accusation that Kiev plotted a sabotage attack in Crimea.
Russian President Vladimir Putin vowed a response.
Russia has moved more military hardware on to the peninsula.
Images of Russian navy exercises in Crimea in response to the saboteur threat were quickly broadcast worldwide.
This week Russia is carrying out more exercises in Crimea to counter the threat of weapons of mass destruction.
Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko has put his military on high alert.
He says the Kremlin fabricated the claim of a sabotage attack by Ukrainian special forces to justify future attacks.
However, almost nothing has changed at the checkpoints in and out of Crimea.
One man from the southern Ukrainian city of Odessa said he went there only to visit his elderly mother who lived there and wouldn't leave.
He said that after she dies, he will stop travelling there.
For Igor, travelling to Crimea to visit relatives, the latest rhetoric is "mostly exaggerated". "
I think what you see on TV about saboteur groups being arrested could be fabricated by either side.
Either side could stage provocations."
With a tennis racket bag over his shoulder, Artyom, a Ukrainian likely in his 20s, says his holiday in Crimea has been pleasant and the people friendly.
He is not alone in that view. "
The Russians say one thing and the Ukrainians another.
I'm not sure whom to believe," says an elderly woman with sunglasses.
When it comes to Russia's tactics and actions toward Ukraine, fact and fiction are often blurred.
Kiev calls this "hybrid warfare", which mixes propaganda with cyber attacks and semi-clandestine operations.
Tamara is driving to Crimea with her chihuahua Charlie, where she owns property.
She might not believe all the rumours in Kiev.
However, she does not trust the Russian version of recent events. "
I think [the Russians] did this on purpose.
But I don't know why they did this during the holiday season.
Everything was fine when I came here in June with my mum."
Tamara's mother-in-law and daughter were going to join her on the trip to Crimea, but because of what they had seen on the news they decided to stay in Kiev.

Across the water from Crimea in the small town of Skadovsk, the melee of swimsuits and food-sellers on the beach is proof that many Ukrainians will simply not travel to Russian-annexed Crimea as a point of principle.
Few seem to notice the Ukrainian National Border Guard soldiers high above in their concrete lookout post at the back of the beach, behind an unseen network of trenches.
For all the political rhetoric of recent days, the fun-loving normality of the summer season in southern Ukraine goes on.

original_chunks: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) has a demanding responsibility enforcing banking laws, regulating financial institutions, and protecting depositors.

Because of the importance of FDIC's work, effective information security controls are essential to ensure that the corporation's systems and information are adequately protected from inadvertent misuse, fraudulent use, or improper disclosure.

As part of its audits of the 2010 financial statements of the Deposit Insurance Fund and the Federal Savings & Loan Insurance Corporation Resolution Fund administrated by FDIC, GAO assessed the effectiveness of the corporation's controls in protecting the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of its financial systems and information.
To conduct the audit, GAO reviewed security policies, procedures, reports, and other documents, tested key financial application controls, and interviewed key FDIC personnel.

Although FDIC had implemented numerous controls in its systems, it had not always implemented access and other controls to protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of its financial systems and information.

FDIC has implemented controls to detect and change default user accounts and passwords in vendor-supplied software, restricted access to network management servers, developed and tested contingency plans for major systems, and improved mainframe logging controls.

However, the corporation had not consistently (1) required strong passwords for financial systems and databases; (2) reviewed user access to financial information in its document sharing system; (3) encrypted financial information in transit and at rest on its network; and (4) protected powerful database accounts and privileges from unauthorized use.
Moreover, FDIC's controls also had other shortcomings related to separating incompatible duties, managing system configurations, and applying patches correctly.
An underlying reason for the information security weaknesses is that FDIC had not always implemented key information security program activities.
On the positive side, FDIC had established and documented a security program and completed actions to correct or mitigate 26 of the 33 previously identified weaknesses reported by GAO.

Instead, they start with an instinctive choice, analyze it, find errors, resolve inconsistencies, and switch between hypotheses.
Thus, they generate a sequence of ideas and follow a thought process leading to a conclusion.

Contrary to this, today's neural
classification models are mostly trained to map an input to one single and
fixed output.
In this paper, we investigate how models can have multiple thoughts.

We take inspiration from
Hegel's dialectics and propose a method that turns an existing classifier's
class prediction (such as the image class forest) into a sequence of
predictions (such as forest $\rightarrow$ tree $\rightarrow$ mushroom).

Concretely, we propose a correction module that is trained to estimate the
model's correctness as well as an iterative prediction update based on the
prediction's gradient.
Our approach results in a dynamic system over class probability distributions.

We evaluate our
method on diverse datasets and tasks from computer vision and natural language
processing.

We observe surprisingly complex but intuitive behavior and
demonstrate that our method (i) can correct misclassifications, (ii)
strengthens model performance, (iii) is robust to high levels of adversarial
attacks, (iv) can increase accuracy up to 4% in a label-distribution-shift
setting and (iv) provides a tool for model interpretability that uncovers model
knowledge which otherwise remains invisible in a single distribution
prediction.

original_chunks: Multivariate time series often have missing values, irregular sampling, and multi-resolution signals, making prediction difficult.

These challenges are especially prevalent in the healthcare domain,
where patients' vital signs and electronic records are collected at different
frequencies and have occasionally missing information due to the imperfections
in equipment or patient circumstances.
Researchers typically address these issues by imputing missing data with mean values and applying sequence models to multivariate signals while ignoring differences in signal resolution.
We introduce a unified model called the Multi-resolution Flexible Irregular Time Series Network (Multi-FIT).

The
building block for Multi-FIT is the FIT network.
The FIT network creates a dense representation at each time step using signal information such as the last observed value, time since the last observed time stamp, and the signal's overall mean.

Vertical FIT (FIT-V) is a variant of FIT which
also models the relationship between different temporal signals while creating
the informative dense representations for the signal.
Multi-FIT uses multiple FIT networks for signal groups at different resolutions, further supporting flexible representation construction.

Our model has three
main contributions: a.) it does not impute values but rather creates
informative representations to provide flexibility to the model for creating
task-specific representations b.) it models the relationship between different
signals in the form of support signals c.) it models different resolutions in
parallel before merging them for the final prediction task.
The FIT, FIT-V, and Multi-FIT networks outperform state-of-the-art models on three predictive tasks, including patient survival forecasting.

original_chunks:
In order to successfully perform tasks specified by natural language
instructions, an artificial agent operating in a visual world needs to map
words, concepts, and actions from the instruction to visual elements in its
environment.
This is called Task-Oriented Grounding.

In this
work, we propose a novel Dynamic Attention Network architecture for the
efficient multi-modal fusion of text and visual representations which can
generate a robust definition of state for the policy learner.
Our model requires no prior knowledge of visual or textual domains and is end to end trainable.
In a 3D environment with continuously changing observations, attention to visual elements is usually highly correlated across consecutive time steps.
We term this as "Dynamic Attention".

In this work,
we show that Dynamic Attention helps in achieving grounding and also aids in
the policy learning objective.
Because many real-world robotic tasks run on a continuously changing observation space, our framework offers a generalized multi-modal fusion module for natural-language-based robotic control.
We also find that applying 1D convolutions to the Gated Attention Hadamard product improves the network’s convergence speed.

We demonstrate that the cell-state of a Long Short Term Memory
(LSTM) is a natural choice for modeling Dynamic Attention and shows through
visualization that the generated attention is very close to how humans tend to
focus on the environment.

original_chunks: In the early 1980s, volatile organic compounds (VOC) were discovered in some of the water systems serving housing areas on Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune.
Exposure to certain VOCs may cause adverse health effects, including cancer.

Since 1991, the Department of Health and Human Services' Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR) has assessed whether people exposed to the contaminated drinking water are likely to suffer adverse health effects.
ATSDR's current study examines whether those exposed in utero are more likely to have developed certain childhood cancers or birth defects.
GAO was asked to testify on its May 11, 2007 report, Defense Health Care: Activities Related to Past Drinking Water Contamination at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune (GAO-07-276).

This testimony presents the report's findings on (1) efforts to identify and address past drinking water contamination, (2) the Department of Defense's (DOD) funding and information provided to ATSDR, and (3) an evaluation of ATSDR's current study design.
GAO reviewed documents, interviewed officials and former residents, and had the National Academy of Sciences convene an expert panel to assess ATSDR's current study.
Efforts to identify and address the past drinking water contamination at Camp Lejeune began in the 1980s, when Navy water testing at Camp Lejeune detected VOCs in some base water systems.

In 1982 and 1983, continued testing identified two VOCs--trichloroethylene (TCE), a metal degreaser, and tetrachloroethylene (PCE), a dry cleaning solvent--in two water systems that served base housing areas, Hadnot Point and Tarawa Terrace.
In 1984 and 1985 a Navy environmental program identified VOCs, such as TCE and PCE, in some of the individual wells serving the Hadnot Point and Tarawa Terrace water systems.
Ten wells were subsequently removed from service.
DOD and North Carolina officials concluded that on- and off-base sources were likely to have caused the contamination.
The start of contamination at Hadnot Point has not been established.
ATSDR estimated that contamination of Tarawa Terrace wells from an off-base dry cleaner began as early as 1957.
Since beginning its Camp Lejeune work in 1991, ATSDR has not consistently received its requested funding and has faced delays in getting information from DOD.

However, ATSDR officials said that although DOD actions likely caused delays and higher costs related to funding and record access, they did not significantly hinder ATSDR's Camp Lejeune-related health studies.
ATSDR officials also said that issues such as limited access to DOD data had to be addressed, but such situations are normal in a study.

Experts on the National Academy of Sciences panel convened for GAO generally agreed that many parts of ATSDR's current study are appropriate, including the study population, exposure time frame, and selected health effects.

Regarding the study's proposed completion date of December 2007, the panel experts had mixed opinions: three of the five panel experts who commented said that the projected date appeared reasonable, while two said that the date might be optimistic.
DOD, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Department of Health and Human Services submitted technical comments on a draft of the May 11, 2007 report, which GAO incorporated as appropriate.

Three members of an ATSDR community assistance panel for Camp Lejeune provided oral comments on issues such as other VOCs that have been detected at Camp Lejeune, and compensation, health benefits, and additional notification for former residents.
GAO focused its review on TCE and PCE because they were identified by ATSDR as the chemicals of primary concern.
GAO's report notes that other VOCs were detected.
GAO incorporated the panel members' comments where appropriate, but some issues were beyond the scope of the report.

Efforts to identify and address the past drinking water contamination at Camp Lejeune began in the 1980s, when Navy water testing at Camp Lejeune detected VOCs in some base water systems.

In 1982 and 1983, continued testing identified two VOCs--trichloroethylene (TCE), a metal degreaser, and tetrachloroethylene (PCE), a dry cleaning solvent--in two water systems that served base housing areas, Hadnot Point and Tarawa Terrace.
In 1984 and 1985 a Navy environmental program identified VOCs, such as TCE and PCE, in some of the individual wells serving the Hadnot Point and Tarawa Terrace water systems during that period.
Ten wells were subsequently removed from service.
DOD and North Carolina officials concluded that on- and off-base sources were likely to have caused the contamination.
The start of contamination at Hadnot Point has not been established with certainty.
ATSDR estimated that contamination of Tarawa Terrace wells from an off-base dry cleaner began as early as 1957, according to its assessment.
Since beginning its Camp Lejeune work in 1991, ATSDR has not consistently received its requested funding and has faced delays in getting needed information from DOD.

However, ATSDR officials said that although DOD actions likely caused delays and higher costs related to funding and record access, they did not significantly hinder ATSDR's Camp Lejeune-related health studies overall.
ATSDR officials also said that issues such as limited access to DOD data had to be addressed, but that such situations are normal in the course of a study.

Experts on the National Academy of Sciences panel convened for GAO generally agreed that many parts of ATSDR's current study are appropriate, including the study population, exposure time frame, and selected health effects under review.

Regarding the study's proposed completion date of December 2007, the panel experts had mixed opinions: three of the five panel experts who commented said that the projected date appeared reasonable, while two said that the date might be optimistic.

DOD, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Department of Health and Human Services submitted technical comments on a draft of the May 11, 2007 report, which GAO incorporated as appropriate into the final report.

Three members of an ATSDR community assistance panel for Camp Lejeune provided oral comments on issues such as other VOCs that have been detected at Camp Lejeune, and compensation, health benefits, and additional notification for former residents.
GAO focused its review on TCE and PCE because they were identified by ATSDR as the chemicals of primary concern in the report.
GAO's report notes that other VOCs were detected.
GAO incorporated the panel members' comments where appropriate, but some issues were beyond the scope of the report.

This Government Accountability Office (GAO) report examines: (1) U.S. agencies' education initiatives and planning; (2) coordination effectiveness among U.S. agencies, host governments, and international donors on basic education; and (3) U.S. agencies' methods for evaluating basic education program outcomes.

In conducting this work, GAO obtained and analyzed relevant agencies' documents and met with U.S. and foreign government officials and nongovernmental organizations, traveling to selected recipient countries.
Several U.S. agencies—USDA, DOD, DOL, State, MCC, USAID, and the Peace Corps—support basic education activities overseas.
State and USAID have strategic goals specific to promoting improved education.
Several other U.S. agencies support basic education-related activities as part of programs that address their broader mission goals.

For example, DOL supports alternative schooling to remove children from exploitative labor, USDA provides school meals, and DOD builds dormitories and educational facilities to improve access for children far from schools.
GAO observed inconsistency in the planning and execution of these agencies' basic education activities.

From 2001 to 2006, there was no government-wide mechanism to facilitate interagency collaboration and, as a result, GAO identified instances where agencies missed opportunities to collaborate and maximize U.S. resources.
In addition, GAO found that the level of U.S. coordination with host governments and other donors in the eight visited countries varied.

Ineffective coordination hinders donors' ability to monitor or assess host governments' progress toward international objectives, such as Education for All by 2015, a key strategic goal for both the Department of State and USAID.

While U.S. agencies GAO reviewed conduct basic education-related programs to achieve different goals, most collect and use output measures, such as the numbers of schools built or children enrolled, to assess and report on results.
USAID is the only agency with an education-specific goal of increasing access to quality basic education.
However, USAID often struggles to acquire valid and reliable data needed to accurately measure improvements in educational quality.
Without this information, agency officials cannot fully determine if the programs are achieving their strategic goals.

This Government Accountability Office (GAO) report provides a comprehensive examination of three key areas: (1) U.S. agencies' initiatives and strategic planning concerning education; (2) the effectiveness of coordination efforts among U.S. agencies, host governments, and international donors regarding basic education programs; and (3) the specific methods U.S. agencies employ for evaluating the outcomes and impacts of their basic education programs.

In conducting this work, GAO obtained and analyzed relevant agencies' documents and met with U.S. and foreign government officials and nongovernmental organizations, traveling to selected recipient countries.
Several United States government agencies—specifically the USDA, DOD, DOL, State, MCC, USAID, and the Peace Corps—are involved in supporting various basic education activities overseas.
Both the Department of State and USAID maintain specific strategic goals that are directly aimed at promoting and improving educational outcomes.
Several other U.S. agencies support basic education-related activities as part of programs that address their broader mission goals.

For example, the Department of Labor (DOL) supports alternative schooling programs designed to remove children from exploitative labor situations, the USDA provides essential school meals, and the DOD constructs dormitories and educational facilities to improve access for children living far from existing schools.
GAO observed a noticeable inconsistency in how these agencies planned and executed their various basic education activities.

During the period from 2001 to 2006, there was an absence of a unified, government-wide mechanism designed to facilitate robust interagency collaboration, and as a direct result, GAO identified multiple instances where agencies did not seize opportunities to collaborate effectively and thereby missed maximizing the utilization of U.S. resources.
In addition, GAO found that the level of U.S. coordination with host governments and other donors in the eight visited countries varied.

Ineffective coordination among stakeholders hinders donors' collective ability to adequately monitor or accurately assess host governments' progress toward achieving critical international objectives, such as the ambitious Education for All by 2015 goal, which represents a key strategic objective for both the Department of State and USAID.

While U.S. agencies GAO reviewed conduct basic education-related programs to achieve different goals, most collect and use output measures, such as the numbers of schools built or children enrolled, to assess and report on results.
USAID stands as the only agency among those reviewed that possesses a specific, dedicated education-focused goal centered on increasing access to quality basic education.
However, USAID frequently encounters difficulties in acquiring the necessary valid and reliable data that is essential to accurately measure documented improvements in educational quality.
Without this information, agency officials cannot fully determine if the programs are achieving their strategic goals.

The system worked on the basis of mixing up the grid a little - Force India's Sergio Perez ended up out of position in 18th place after the team miscalculated the timing of his final run, leaving him not enough time to complete it before the elimination clock timed him out.

original_chunks: Pursuant to a congressional request, GAO provided information on the Department of Veterans Affairs' (VA) provision of health care services to Gulf War veterans, focusing on: (1) the number of veterans VA and the Department of Defense (DOD) report as suffering from Gulf War-related illnesses and the criteria used to identify these illnesses; (2) how VA diagnoses, counsels, treats, and monitors Gulf War veterans for the health problems they report; and (3) Gulf War veterans' satisfaction with the health care they receive from VA.

GAO noted that: (1) while the number of Persian Gulf War veterans who participated in the military operations known as Desert Shield and Desert Storm is well established at almost 700,000, the number who actually suffer, or believe they suffer, from illnesses related to their Gulf War service remains uncertain 7 years after the war; (2) the primary difficulty in assessing the impact of such illnesses lies in the fact that the link between the veterans' symptoms and the causes of those symptoms has not yet been identified scientifically; (3) thus, while some data on Gulf War veterans' symptoms have been collected and categorized, it is not yet known whether the symptoms reported are the direct result of the veterans' Gulf War service; (4) combined, VA and DOD report, however, that about

100,000 Gulf War veterans have requested Persian Gulf Registry examinations because of war-related health concerns; (5) in response to a variety of symptoms and illnesses reported by Gulf War veterans, VA implemented a program in 1992 to help them receive VA health care; (6) this free diagnostic and referral process has two stages: (a) an initial medical history and a physical examination with basic laboratory testing; and (b) if needed, further evaluation through specialist consultation and additional symptom-specific testing; (7) 212 VA facilities offer the Registry program to Gulf War veterans; (8) however, VA's guidance regarding the evaluation and diagnosis of Gulf War veterans is not being consistently implemented in some of its medical facilities; (9) while VA records show that thousands of veterans

remain undiagnosed, only about 500 veterans have been sent to referral centers for additional evaluations, as recommended by the Registry guidance; (10) mandated personal counseling of veterans often does not occur, and the form letters sent to veterans at the completion of the Registry examination do not always sufficiently explain test results or diagnoses, often leaving veterans frustrated and confused; (11) VA's guidance provides that Registry physicians are responsible for giving veterans medical examinations and necessary treatment; (12) VA has not fully developed and implemented an integrated diagnostic and treatment program to meet the health care needs of Gulf War veterans; (13) VA's diagnostic and treatment implementation problems are reflected by Gulf War veterans' general dissatisfaction with their health care; and (14) based on GAO's nationwide
survey, over one half of the veterans who received the Registry examination in 1996 and 1997 were dissatisfied with the examination they received.

original_chunks: Frank and Mary Finlay bought Molly in November 2015 thinking she was female.
But they soon noticed she lifted her leg unusually when urinating and asked the vets to investigate.
They found that Molly had male testicles, which had not descended, and female genitalia with a poorly-formed "vestigial" penis. "
Some might call it intersex and others non-binary, since she is neither male nor female, but the correct scientific term is that she is a male pseudohermaphrodite," says vet Ross Allan.
He operated on Molly once it was clear the anatomical differences were causing problems.
Mr Allan told BBC Scotland's Kaye Adams Programme: "It is very rare. "
In the literature there have been about 15 cases published in total. "
In 15 years in this profession, I have seen this only in Molly and no other dog."
The Glasgow vet says his colleagues in the profession had not come across it either.
Mr Finlay told Kaye Adams: "When we got Molly we believed her to be a bitch. "
I noticed she would squat to urinate indoors, but outside she would lift her leg."
He mentioned it to the vet at Mr Allan's Pollokshaws surgery and they raised possibility of Molly being hermaphrodite.
Mr Finlay says: "They did scans and x-rays and eventually she was operated on in May 2016 at six months old."
The vet says they diagnosed Molly early but delayed operating until she had grown.
He says: "We did x-rays to see where Molly's urethra went - the tube from her bladder to the outside world - and its route. "
We found that although Molly appeared female, her urethra took the path it would in a male dog. "
She did not have a properly formed penis. "
She actually had the female external genitalia, as it were, but in the male formation. "
That was the problem.
It was abnormal anatomy and was becoming inflamed."
The vet says that as time went on Molly "was starting to get interested in soft cushions" and behave more like a male dog. "
But not having the proper anatomy for that was also likely to cause further problems," he said. "
The concern was that without surgery, this would have worsened and become more severe over time."
The operation removed the "vestigial" penis and created a female opening in Molly's groin.
Mrs Finlay says: "It was a worry because it was big operation. "
She was only six months old.
She was very small.
When we got her she was only 11in long and six inches high.
She was tiny."
Mrs Finlay says: "The surgery was quite nerve-wracking.
My daughter Joy was saying 'don't worry mum everything's going to be fine'. "
I lay awake at night worrying. "
When she came home with us she was at the bottom of our bed, with her own blanket and she lay there crying."
There was some haemorrhaging, but Molly stayed with the vet for several days and fully recovered. "
That was very scary, but she came through it," says Mrs Finlay.
It has now been almost a year since Molly's operation.
Mrs Finlay says: "She is a fantastic wee dog and great with the grandchildren.
Everyone that comes in gets their ears licked.
She just runs up to people and licks their ears."
Mr Allan says: "Molly is Molly and she is happy and fit and healthy, that is the main thing."

original_chunks: As amended, the Clean Air Act requires certain areas with especially poor air quality to use a special gasoline blend to reduce volatile organic compounds (VOC) and nitrogen oxides (NOx), and to use an oxygenate such as ethanol.
In less severely polluted areas, the Act allows states, with EPA approval, to require the use of other special blends as part of their effort to meet air quality standards.
GAO agreed to answer the following: (1) To what extent are special gasoline blends used in the United States and how, if at all, is this use expected to change in the future? (
2) What effect has the use of these blends had on reducing vehicle emissions and improving overall air quality? (
3) What is the effect of these blends on the gasoline supply? (
4) How do these blends affect gasoline prices?
No consensus exists on the total number of gasoline blends in the United States, but GAO identified 11 distinct special blends in operation during summer 2004.

original_chunks: Aligned image and text encoders have significantly advanced zero-shot image classification.
This research aims to advance zero-shot object detection, which identifies novel objects without bounding box or mask labels.

We propose ViLD, a training method via Vision and Language
knowledge Distillation.
We transfer knowledge from a pre-trained zero-shot image classification model (e.g., CLIP) to a two-stage detector (e.g., Mask R-CNN).
Our method aligns the detector's region embeddings with text and image embeddings from the pre-trained model.
We use text embeddings, generated by inputting category names into the pre-trained text encoder, as the detection classifier.

We then minimize the distance between the region
embeddings and image embeddings, obtained by feeding region proposals into the
pre-trained image encoder.
During inference, we integrate text embeddings for new categories into the detection classifier for zero-shot detection.

We
benchmark the performance on LVIS dataset by holding out all rare categories as
novel categories.

ViLD obtains 16.1 mask AP$_r$ with a Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50
FPN) for zero-shot detection, outperforming the supervised counterpart by 3.8.

The model can directly transfer to other datasets, achieving 72.2 AP$_{50}$,
36.6 AP and 11.8 AP on PASCAL VOC, COCO and Objects365, respectively.
modified_chunks: Aligned image and text encoders have led to substantial improvements and made significant advancements in the field of zero-shot image classification.

This particular research endeavor focuses on the goal of advancing zero-shot object detection, which involves the crucial task of identifying novel objects in images without requiring explicit bounding box or mask labels during training.

We propose ViLD, a training method via Vision and Language
knowledge Distillation.
We accomplish this by transferring valuable knowledge from an already pre-trained zero-shot image classification model, such as CLIP, to a robust two-stage detector architecture like Mask R-CNN.
Our developed method meticulously aligns the detector's learned region embeddings with both the text and image embeddings derived from the powerful pre-trained model.
We strategically utilize text embeddings, which are effectively generated by inputting various category names into the pre-trained text encoder, to serve as the detection classifier for our system.

We then minimize the distance between the region
embeddings and image embeddings, obtained by feeding region proposals into the
pre-trained image encoder.

During the inference phase, we seamlessly integrate text embeddings corresponding to new and previously unseen categories directly into the detection classifier to enable effective zero-shot detection capabilities.

We rigorously benchmark the performance of our proposed method on the comprehensive LVIS dataset by intentionally holding out all of its rare categories, treating them as novel categories for evaluation purposes.

ViLD obtains 16.1 mask AP$_r$ with a Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50
FPN) for zero-shot detection, outperforming the supervised counterpart by 3.8.

The model can directly transfer to other datasets, achieving 72.2 AP$_{50}$,
36.6 AP and 11.8 AP on PASCAL VOC, COCO and Objects365, respectively.

Business rates and the new national living wage are among extra outgoings.

Tesco's shares fell 3% during midday trading on Tuesday. "

This figure represents our highest tax burden, triple the OECD average.

original_chunks: Multimodal sentiment analysis determines emotional states by analyzing communication forms like speech, tone, and facial expressions.
It has become a vital and evolving area within natural language processing.

Much research focuses on modeling the complex
intra- and inter-modal interactions between different communication channels.

However, current multimodal models with strong performance are often
deep-learning-based techniques and work like black boxes.
It remains unclear how models use multimodal information for sentiment predictions.
Despite recent advances in explaining machine learning models, they mostly target unimodal scenarios (e.g., images, sentences), with little research on multimodal models.
In this paper, we introduce M2Lens, an interactive visual analytics system to visualize and explain multimodal models for sentiment analysis.

M2Lens provides explanations
on intra- and inter-modal interactions at the global, subset, and local levels.

Specifically, it summarizes the influence of three typical interaction types
(i.e., dominance, complement, and conflict) on the model predictions.
Moreover, M2Lens identifies common and impactful multimodal features and supports comprehensive exploration of model behaviors across language, acoustic, and visual modalities.

Through two case studies and expert interviews, we
demonstrate our system can help users gain deep insights into the multimodal
models for sentiment analysis.

original_chunks: Spatial time series forecasting is important in many applications, especially environmental and transportation domains.
These tasks are difficult due to distinct spatial, short-term, and long-term patterns, and the curse of dimensionality.

In this paper, we propose
a deep neural network framework for large-scale spatial time series forecasting
problems.

We explicitly designed the neural network architecture for capturing
various types of patterns.

In preprocessing, a time series decomposition method
is applied to separately feed short-term, long-term and spatial patterns into
different components of a neural network.

A fuzzy clustering method finds
cluster of neighboring time series based on similarity of time series
residuals; as they can be meaningful short-term patterns for spatial time
series.
In the neural network, each kernel in the multi-kernel convolution layer is assigned to a time series cluster to extract short-term features from neighboring areas.

The output of convolution layer is concatenated
by trends and followed by convolution-LSTM layer to capture long-term patterns
in larger regional areas.
To handle missing data robustly, an unsupervised pretrained denoising autoencoder reconstructs the model output during fine-tuning.

Experimental results show the
model outperforms baseline and state of the art models in a traffic flow
prediction dataset.

Yet, despite success with time-series data [1], [2], many time series are multiscale, and a single-hidden-layer RC model may struggle to capture that structure.

In this paper, we
propose a novel hierarchical reservoir computing framework we call Deep Echo
State Networks (Deep-ESNs).

The most distinctive feature of a Deep-ESN is its
ability to deal with time series through hierarchical projections.

Specifically, when an input time series is projected into the high-dimensional
echo-state space of a reservoir, a subsequent encoding layer (e.g., a PCA,
autoencoder, or a random projection) can project the echo-state representations
into a lower-dimensional space.
These reduced representations are then processed by an additional ESN.

By using projection layers and encoding layers
alternately in the hierarchical framework, a Deep-ESN can not only attenuate
the effects of the collinearity problem in ESNs, but also fully take advantage
of the temporal kernel property of ESNs to explore multiscale dynamics of time
series.
To combine multiscale representations from each reservoir, we connect every encoding layer to the final output layer.

Theoretical
analyses prove that stability of a Deep-ESN is guaranteed by the echo state
property (ESP), and the time complexity is equivalent to a conventional ESN.
Experiments on several synthetic and real-world time series show that Deep-ESNs model multiscale dynamics and outperform both standard ESNs and earlier hierarchical ESN approaches.

original_chunks: In 1996, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) launched a human capital reform initiative under one of the federal government's most flexible human capital management frameworks, with broad exemptions from title 5 laws governing federal civilian personnel management.

GAO was asked (1) to examine the changes FAA initiated in its reform effort, including whether they required an exemption from title 5 and their implementation status; (2) determine the effects of the reform effort according to available data and the views of FAA officials, managers, and employees; and (3) assess the extent to which FAA's reform effort incorporated elements that are important to effective human capital management.
In 1996, FAA initiated human capital reform initiatives in three broad areas, some of which required exemption from title 5, and some of which have been fully implemented.
FAA has not yet completed implementation of some key initiatives.
For example, FAA's new compensation system remains unimplemented for about one-quarter of the agency's workforce--those staff whose unions have not reached agreements with FAA.

FAA's need to implement initiatives among a workforce with a wide range of skills and to negotiate changes with multiple unions were among factors that affected the pace and extent of reform implementation.
FAA had limited data to assess the effects of its reform effort.
Although FAA human capital officials cited positive effects from the agency's reform effort, managers and employees GAO interviewed were generally less favorable.

FAA's lack of sufficient empirical data on the effects of its human capital initiatives shows it has not fully incorporated key elements of effective human capital management into its overall reform effort.
These elements include data collection and analysis, performance goals and measures, and linkage of reform goals to program goals.

FAA human resource management officials said that the agency should have spent more time to develop baseline data and performance measures before implementing the broad range of reforms but that establishing these elements was a complex and difficult task.
FAA also has not sufficiently linked reform goals to the organization's overall program goals.

GAO found that evaluations of FAA's human capital reform effort have consistently cited the absence of these elements, yet FAA has not set specific steps and time frames to implement and use them for evaluation.
Incorporating these elements could also help FAA build accountability into its human capital management.

The Office of Cuba Broadcasting (OCB) transmits its Radio and TV Marti content through various methods, each of which faces differing levels of jamming and interference from the Cuban government's efforts to block the signals.

Specifically, less than 2 percent of respondents to telephone surveys since 2003 reported tuning in to Radio or TV Marti during the past week.

The International Broadcasting Bureau (IBB), which serves as OCB's direct supervisory body, utilizes an annual program review process as its primary mechanism for evaluating OCB's adherence to established journalistic standards and principles.

While IBB officials report that the quality of OCB programming has improved in recent years, IBB reviews since 2003 have recommended improving adherence to certain journalistic standards, particularly in the areas of balance and objectivity.

Though IBB's current review process provides valuable feedback regarding programming quality, we identified several operational deficiencies, including insufficient training for reviewers and a lack of clear operational guidance for conducting assessments.

OCB and IBB have implemented various steps and measures designed to ensure that U.S. government broadcasting complies with relevant domestic laws and international standards, but despite these efforts, certain concerns about compliance continue to persist.

To comply with specific U.S. law prohibiting domestic dissemination, OCB and IBB have made attempts to limit the distribution of OCB program content within the United States, yet these broadcasts still manage to reach U.S. audiences through alternative channels like the internet and satellite transmissions.

Additionally, it was noted that a commercial television station that aired OCB programs was observed to have broadcast inappropriate commercial advertisements during the time slots when the OCB content was being shown.

Moreover, an independent international organization has previously determined that OCB's television broadcasts cause harmful technical interference to the legitimate broadcasts of the Cuban government, but the U.S. government has not yet taken concrete action to address or rectify this identified problem.
Despite some efforts by BBG and OCB, oversight entities have identified problems such as poor communication by OCB management and low employee morale.

For example, the Office of Cuba Broadcasting currently lacks formal, established mechanisms and structured channels for effectively communicating with its employees or for systematically obtaining essential information and feedback from them.

original_chunks: President Rodrigo Duterte aims to pursue peace, with an estimated 30,000 fatalities in the conflict since the 1960s.
BBC Monitoring's Mark Wilson examines the challenges ahead.
The Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) began its armed struggle in the late 1960s.
The organization seeks to overthrow the government through guerrilla warfare.
The insurgency was founded by academic, author and poet Jose Maria Sison.
The CPP's armed wing, the New People's Army (NPA), has about 4,000 fighters, down from 26,000 in the 1980s.
The NPA has conducted killings, bombings and hostage-taking, collecting "revolutionary taxes" from businesses in controlled areas.
Both the CPP and NPA were labeled as foreign terrorist organizations by the US in 2002.
The rebels strongly oppose the US military presence in the Philippines and have in the past killed American service personnel stationed in the country.
Since the 1980s they have engaged in talks with successive governments, but peace remains elusive.
Mr Duterte wants to end the insurgency and has said he is willing to "walk the extra mile" for peace.
He has restarted the peace process with two formal discussions since taking office.
The president has attempted to win the rebels' trust through a series of confidence-building measures.
These include appointing rebel sympathisers to his cabinet, releasing high-ranking rebels from prison and offering land to NPA members if talks succeed.
The rebels have responded by releasing police officers they were holding hostage.
Both sides have announced unilateral ceasefires, but no joint agreement has been reached.
The ceasefires have been marred by the killings of soldiers and rebels.
Government officials accused the CPP of being unable to control its armed wing after four soldiers were killed in an NPA landmine attack in July.
The attack led Mr Duterte to temporarily suspend the government ceasefire.
Days later, an NPA rebel was killed in a battle with the military in Surigao del Norte province.
The rebels, who claim they will not surrender their arms even if a deal is reached, accuse the military of using Mr Duterte's drug war as a pretext for operations during the ceasefire.
A real sticking point in recent months has been the issue of freeing around 400 detained rebels.
The CPP demands a general amnesty for these rebels as part of negotiations.
After Mr Duterte refused, insisting that the rebels must first agree to a joint ceasefire deal, the rebels accused him of "capriciously changing his mind" on the issue.
Since the last round of talks in October, the rebels have also taken issue with some of Mr Duterte's policies at home and abroad.
They have criticised both his warming relations with Russia and China and his move to allow a hero's burial for late dictator Ferdinand Marcos.
At the upcoming talks on 18 January in Rome, both sides aim to reach a bilateral ceasefire deal.
That the talks have got this far demonstrates the desire for peace on both sides, but delays in granting amnesties to detained rebels is threatening to derail negotiations.
Comprehensive social and economic reforms proposed by the rebels, which the CPP describes as the core of the talks, are still to be agreed.

original_chunks: In June 2007, SBA established the Patriot Express Pilot Loan Program within its 7(a) loan guarantee program to provide small businesses owned and operated by veterans and other eligible members of the military community access to capital.
Through Patriot Express, SBA guarantees individual small business loans that lenders originate.
GAO was asked to evaluate the program.

This report examines (1) trends in the volume and performance of Patriot Express and related SBA loan programs; (2) the effect of the program on eligible members of the military community; and (3) SBA internal controls to ensure that only eligible borrowers participate.

GAO analyzed performance and costs of Patriot Express and other similar SBA loan programs from 2007 through 2012; interviewed selected borrowers, lenders, and veteran service organizations; and reviewed SBA internal control guidance on borrower eligibility.

Patriot Express loans valued at about $703 million have shown a higher default rate compared to loans under the SBA's other related loan guarantee programs, with losses for Patriot Express surpassing its income.
Except for loans approved in 2007, Patriot Express loans have demonstrated a higher default rate than loans made under SBA's main 7(a) program or SBA Express.
The Patriot Express program's overall default rate was significantly higher for smaller loans, especially for loans below $25,000 (20 percent).
Additionally, one lender accounted for more than 64 percent of these smaller loans and experienced higher default rates than the remaining lenders.
From 2007 through 2012, the Patriot Express program suffered losses exceeding its income by $31.1 million (not considering future fee revenues or funds recovered from loans in default).

Selected borrowers, lenders, and veteran service organizations highlighted various benefits and challenges of the Patriot Express program, yet SBA has not assessed its impact on eligible members of the military community.
Borrowers and lenders said that some benefits of the program were that it helped veterans expand their businesses and allowed them to take advantage of the streamlined application process.
Some challenges they identified were low awareness of the program and which lenders participated in the program.
In 2010, SBA extended the Patriot Express pilot through 2013 to allow time to evaluate the program's effect.
To date, SBA has not evaluated the program or established a plan of what it intends to do to evaluate it.
SBA officials told us that they focused their resources on evaluating 7(a) loans because there are many more of them and, therefore, they pose a greater risk to SBA than Patriot Express loans.
Alongside Patriot Express, SBA has previously launched other pilot programs that it has not evaluated.

GAO has found that a program evaluation gives an agency the opportunity to refine program design, assess if program operations have resulted in the desired benefits, and, for pilots, determine whether to make the programs permanent.

Without conducting evaluations of pilot programs, SBA lacks the information needed to assess their performance and their effects on eligible participants and decide whether to extend these programs, including Patriot Express.

SBA's internal controls over lenders may not offer sufficient assurance that Patriot Express loans are only made to eligible members of the military community and that only these members benefit from loan proceeds.
SBA depends on lenders to verify and document borrower eligibility at the time of loan approval.
One of SBA's controls over lenders' compliance with eligibility requirements involves sampling loan files during examinations of the 7(a) program, but few Patriot Express loans are reviewed.
Patriot Express is intended to assist only eligible members of the military community and SBA officials told us that they expect borrowers to maintain eligibility after the loan is disbursed.
However, SBA has not established procedures for lenders to provide reasonable assurance that borrowers maintain this eligibility.
Federal internal control standards and GAO's fraud-prevention framework suggest that ongoing monitoring is a crucial element of an effective internal control system.
Without enhanced internal controls, particularly with respect to monitoring of borrowers, SBA lacks assurance that Patriot Express loans are serving only eligible borrowers.

original_chunks: Since its inception in 1970 with the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA), the U.S. government's framework for preventing, detecting, and prosecuting money laundering has expanded through additional legislation.

The BSA was designed to prevent financial institutions from transferring or depositing criminally sourced funds and to provide law enforcement agencies a documented record for investigations into potential money laundering.
The USA PATRIOT Act enacted the most recent updates in October 2001, broadening antimoney laundering (AML) obligations to additional financial service providers previously outside the BSA.

GAO was asked to testify on its previous work and the ongoing work it is doing for the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the depository institution regulators' BSA examination and enforcement process.
In recent years, GAO has issued a number of reports dealing with regulatory oversight of anti-money laundering activities of financial institutions.
In 1998, GAO issued a report regarding Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network's (FinCEN) role in administering the BSA, which updated information on civil penalties for BSA violations.
One focus was the Secretary of the Treasury's 1994 mandate to delegate the authority to assess civil money penalties for BSA violations to federal banking regulatory agencies.
GAO noted the delegation had not been made and said FinCEN feared bank regulators might assess fewer BSA penalties and instead rely on their non-BSA authorities under their own statutes.
Also in 1998, GAO reported on the activities of Raul Salinas, the brother of the former President of Mexico.
Mr. Salinas is alleged to have laundered Mexico-origin funds through Citibank into accounts held by its affiliates in Switzerland and the United Kingdom.

GAO determined that Mr. Salinas was able to transfer $90 - $100 million between 1992 and 1994 by using a private banking relationship structured through Citibank New York in 1992 and effectively disguise the funds' source and destination, thus breaking the funds' paper trail.
In 2001, GAO issued a report on changes in BSA examination coverage for certain securities broker-dealers.

At that time, not all broker-dealers had to file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), but brokerdealer subsidiaries of depository institutions and their parent holding companies were required to submit SARs under banking regulators' oversight.
After the 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, GAO found these broker-dealers were no longer covered by examinations assessing SAR compliance.
After the USA PATRIOT Act was enacted and a final rule took effect on July 31, 2002, all broker-dealers had to report.
GAO is currently studying the depository institution regulators' BSA examination and enforcement process for the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

The objectives include determining how the regulators' risk-focused examinations assess BSA compliance, the extent to which the regulators identify BSA and AML violations and take supervisory actions, and the consistency of BSA compliance examination procedures and interpretation of violations across regulators.
GAO plans to determine whether and to what extent regulators curtailed BSA compliance examinations and the bases for these decisions.
GAO plans to monitor supervisory measures used to address identified violations.
GAO will assess whether changes occur, and to what extent, due to Treasury not delegating authority to assess BSA compliance penalties to banking regulators, as required by statute.
GAO will contact government and business stakeholders to better understand their perspectives on BSA examination compliance.

Researchers have used machine learning with manually designed features for seizure prediction.
However, complex machine learning methods make choosing optimal models or features difficult.

Deep Learning methods
are beneficial in the sense of automatic feature extraction.

One of the
roadblocks for accurate seizure prediction is scarcity of epileptic seizure
data.

This paper addresses this problem by proposing a deep convolutional
generative adversarial network to generate synthetic EEG samples.

We use two
methods to validate synthesized data namely, one-class SVM and a new proposal
which we refer to as convolutional epileptic seizure predictor (CESP).

Another
objective of our study is to evaluate performance of well-known deep learning
models (e.g., VGG16, VGG19, ResNet50, and Inceptionv3) by training models on
augmented data using transfer learning with average time of 10 min between true
prediction and seizure onset.
Our CESP model achieved 78.11% and 88.21% sensitivities, with 0.27/h and 0.14/h FPRs, respectively, when trained on synthetic data and tested on Epilepsyecosystem and CHB-MIT datasets.

in patient-specific manner provides highest accuracy with sensitivity of 90.03%
and 0.03 FPR/h which was achieved using Inceptionv3, and that augmenting data
with samples generated from DCGAN increased prediction results of our CESP
model and Inceptionv3 by 4-5% as compared to state-of-the-art traditional
augmentation techniques.
Finally, CESP's prediction results using augmented data exceed chance level for both datasets.

Most attacks, such as SQL injection and XSS, rely on HTTP for transmission.

Therefore, it is crucial to develop an
intelligent solution that would allow to effectively detect and filter out
anomalies in HTTP traffic.

Currently, most of the anomaly detection systems are
either rule-based or trained using manually selected features.
We propose using modern unsupervised language models to embed HTTP requests and classify anomalies.
The solution is inspired by NLP methods like Doc2Vec, which can better understand HTTP messages and improve intrusion detection efficiency.
We aim to generate a suitable embedding space and focus on the interpretability of the model.
We chose RoBERTa, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not been applied to this problem before.
To evaluate the solution under real-world conditions, we trained the model using only legitimate traffic.

We also try to explain the
results based on clusters that occur in the vectorized requests space and a
simple logistic regression classifier.

We compared our approach with the
similar, previously proposed methods.

We evaluate the feasibility of our method
on three different datasets: CSIC2010, CSE-CIC-IDS2018 and one that we prepared
ourselves.

The results we show are comparable to others or better, and most
importantly - interpretable.

original_chunks: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has achieved remarkable results in many complex environments by integrating with Deep Neural Networks (DNNs).
Meanwhile, Genetic Algorithms (GAs), often viewed as a rival to RL, had limited success scaling to the DNNs needed for challenging tasks.
Rather than a strict dichotomy, evolution and learning in the physical world are complementary, continuously interacting processes.

The recently proposed Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (ERL) framework has
demonstrated mutual benefits to performance when combining the two methods.
However, ERL has not fully addressed the scalability problem of GAs.
In this paper, we show this problem arises from the unfortunate combination of a simple genetic encoding for DNNs and conventional biologically inspired variation operators.
With these encodings, the standard operators are disruptive and cause catastrophic forgetting of traits acquired by the networks.

We propose a novel algorithm called Proximal
Distilled Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning (PDERL) that is characterised by
a hierarchical integration between evolution and learning.

The main innovation
of PDERL is the use of learning-based variation operators that compensate for
the simplicity of the genetic representation.
Unlike traditional operators, our methods satisfy the functional requirements of variation operators when applied to directly encoded DNNs.

We evaluate PDERL in five robot locomotion settings
from the OpenAI gym.

Our method outperforms ERL, as well as two
state-of-the-art RL algorithms, PPO and TD3, in all tested environments.

original_chunks:
There is a large literature explaining why AdaBoost is a successful
classifier.
The AdaBoost literature emphasizes classifier margins and views boosting as optimizing an exponential likelihood function.
Nonetheless, it has been claimed that current explanations do not cover every aspect.

A random forest is another popular ensemble method for which there
is substantially less explanation in the literature.
We offer a new perspective on AdaBoost and random forests, arguing that they succeed for largely the same underlying reasons.
Although both classifiers have similar predictive accuracy, random forests should not be seen as a mere optimization scheme.

Rather, random forests is a self-averaging,
interpolating algorithm which creates what we denote as a "spikey-smooth"
classifier, and we view AdaBoost in the same light.

We conjecture that both
AdaBoost and random forests succeed because of this mechanism.

We provide a
number of examples and some theoretical justification to support this
explanation.
We thus dispute the usual view that boosting for classification must rely on regularization or early stopping and is confined to low-complexity learners like decision stumps.
We therefore conclude that boosting should be used like random forests, with large decision trees and without direct regularization or early stopping.

original_chunks: Questions have arisen about whether parents with limited English proficiency have difficulty accessing child care and early education programs for their children.
Research suggests high-quality early care can greatly improve young children's school readiness.

GAO was asked to examine (1) these children's participation in Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) and Head Start programs, (2) barriers these families face in accessing programs, (3) assistance from selected state and local entities, and (4) actions the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has taken to help ensure access.

To obtain this information, GAO analyzed program and national survey data, interviewed officials in 5 states and 11 counties, held 12 focus groups with mothers with limited English proficiency, and interviewed experts and HHS officials.

HHS's Child Care Bureau (CCB) did not have information on the total enrollment in CCDF programs of children whose parents had limited English proficiency, but data collected by its Office of Head Start in 2003 showed that about 13 percent of parents whose children were in Head Start reported having limited English proficiency.

The most recent (1998) national survey data showed that children of parents with limited English proficiency were less likely than other children to receive financial assistance for child care from a social service or welfare agency or to be in Head Start, after controlling for selected characteristics.
Eighty-eight percent of these children were Hispanic, and their results differed from Asian children.

GAO's review of focus groups and site visit interviews found that mothers with limited English proficiency faced several difficulties, including limited knowledge of available assistance, language barriers in the application process, and problems communicating with English-speaking providers.

Some of the challenges that low-income parents with limited English proficiency experienced, such as lack of transportation and shortage of subsidized child care slots, were common to other low-income families.
The majority of state and local agencies that we visited offered some oral and written language assistance, such as bilingual staff or translated applications.
In most locations visited, agencies also took steps to increase the number of providers able to communicate with parents.
Officials reported challenges in serving parents with limited English proficiency, including difficulties recruiting qualified bilingual staff.
Some officials indicated that additional information on cost-effective strategies to serve this population would facilitate their efforts.
HHS provided guidance, translated materials, and technical assistance to grantees to help them serve children of parents with limited English proficiency.

The Office of Head Start reviewed programs' assessments of their communities' needs and conducted formal monitoring reviews, but could not ensure review teams consistently evaluated grantees' compliance with language-access standards.

CCB reviewed states' plans on the use of CCDF funds generally and investigated specific complaints, but had no mechanism for reviewing how and whether states provide access to CCDF subsidies for eligible children of parents with limited English proficiency.

original_chunks: When you turn sixteen, you're filled with anticipation and anxst of getting your liscence, and furthermore a car!
I've certainly been there.
But what exactly makes getting a car so appealing?
Well, other than the new found sense of freedom.
Not much.
Automobile use rose rapidly from the 1900's and is now steadily declining.
Why?
Less stress, less pollution, and more excerise.
These things alone may not be enough to convince you, so let's jump into the facts.
First off, getting rid of that car in your driveway will greatly lower your stress.
As a result, 70 percent of Vauban's families own no cars, and 57 percent sold one to move here.
Owning a car used to cause me constant stress.
I'm much happier this way.
On reflection, this makes perfect sense.
When you have a car you have to worry about gas prices, payments, and fixes.
In contrast, if you live without a car, those concerns do not affect you.
So, therefore your stress decreases and your happiness can go up to an all time high.
When you have one less bill each month it truly does leave an impact.
Secondly, pollution and smog are major issues within our control.
Who is to blame?
We are.
Fumes and smoke are building up in our atmosphere with nowhere to go.
Our cars are a huge part of it. "
Diesel fuel was blamed" in France for their smog layers.
Cold nights and warm days trapped car emissions under layers of warm air.
We must end this problem.
It is harming our planet.
It will keep destroying it until we change and act to stop it.
It's up to us, and we can't ignore it.
The problem will not just go away.
It will not fix itself.

But America's love affair with its vehicles seems to be cooling."
So, it's not as big of a deal as it used to be.
Not everyone needs or wants to have a car anymore. "

When you decide that you don't want a car, you're benefiting from it and the future is benefiting from it.
Taking the next step seems a bit out of reach but we can make it.

Show the world it does more harm than good. "

It takes just one person to start a movement.

original_chunks: Stuart Armstrong put the hosts ahead with a 25-yard drive through a crowd.
Jordan Jones drew Killie level against the run of play after the break but Scott Sinclair soon made it 2-1.
James Forrest headed in the third to seal Celtic's win and end Killie's top-six hopes.
With Partick Thistle beating Motherwell 1-0 at Firhill, they cannot be caught in the race for a top-six berth.
Lee McCulloch's side gave the champions a guard of honour as they took to the field and the interim boss showed Celtic further respect by deploying a five-man defence.
Gary Dicker, Iain Wilson and Scott Boyd filled the central roles with Luke Hendrie and Greg Taylor occupying the full-back berths.
The formation hindered Celtic early, but Killie's clearances kept falling to green-and-white players.
Chances eventually came for the hosts, with Sinclair firing wide from Forrest's cross before Callum McGregor's deflected effort was tipped over by keeper Freddie Woodman.
The breakthrough came midway through the first half, with March player of the month making the difference.
Armstrong tried a long-range shot, and it grazed something before slipping past Woodman for his 14th goal of the season.

Last ditch tackles from Wilson and Boyd denied McGregor and Armstrong before Kieran Tierney sent a left foot volley wide of the target as the home side were unable to increase their lead before the interval.
At times it was like a training game for Celtic as they maximised possession and Killie sat back and hoped to hit them on the break.
The tactic worked as the Rugby Park men squared it against the run of play.
Conor Sammon's attempted shot broke into the path of Jones and his effort from 16 yards took a deflection to beat Craig Gordon.
That goal sparked Celtic and, from Armstrong's free kick, Boyata's header was turned across by McGregor for Sinclair to tap in from close range.
Moussa Dembele made an instant impact as a substitute, setting up Celtic's third.
The rebound came off the Killie keeper's left post, and Forrest smashed it into the net from two yards.
The result extends Celtic's unbeaten domestic run to 39 games as Killie experienced their first defeat away from home in their last seven games.
Celtic manager Brendan Rodgers: "I thought it was an outstanding team performance.
We played our shape very very well, the quality of the movement, the speed.
It was difficult in the beginning because Lee (McCulloch) obviously set his team out very tight in their organisation in a real low position and that's always difficult to break down. "
But we showed quality and great patience, and I also applaud the crowd as they're seeing what we're trying to do—they're not getting frustrated, and we have to be patient at times. "
Our only mistake was from the counter-attack for the goal, but otherwise we showed great energy throughout the game today.
We got three goals and with a bit more luck we could have had another one or two."
Interim Kilmarnock boss Lee McCulloch: "I thought first half we were too deep, stood off the game too much and allowed Celtic a little bit too much respect.
Second half we changed the system and decided to go a little bit higher up the pitch. "
I'm delighted with the way the boys played and the character and concentration they showed for most of the game. "
We get back in the game and gather a little bit of momentum then we just switch off for a set play as we have done a couple of times this season - that's the most disappointing part of the day. "
Did we deserve to win today?
But I'm pleased the players showed character, kept the ball moving and, on another day, we might have taken something from it."

We get back in the game and gather a little bit of momentum then we just switch off for a set play as we have done a couple of times this season - that's the most disappointing part of the day. "

The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) has certainly implemented numerous information security controls to protect its key financial systems; however, the presence of remaining weaknesses still poses risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and overall availability of its financial systems and the sensitive information they manage.

Throughout the entirety of 2015, the corporation consistently maintained a high priority on ensuring the robust security of its critical financial data and the supporting systems that facilitate its operations.
Key among its actions were improving controls for identifying and authenticating the identity of users and improving controls for authorizing users' access.
Nevertheless, despite these efforts, the FDIC still continues to face a number of unresolved vulnerabilities within its information security framework.

For example, the corporation (1) did not have an effective process for recertifying user access rights to several systems supporting the corporation's financial processing and (2) had not yet applied critical patches to mitigate known vulnerabilities in third party software on systems supporting financial processing.

While the corporation had in place an extensive information security program framework designed to protect its assets, certain specific elements within this framework were regrettably not fully implemented or consistently applied.

For example, the corporation did not (1) fully document and implement procedures for performing system access requests, assignments, and removal and (2) have a policy for monitoring critical file changes.
In addition, FDIC had yet to fully address 9 previously-reported weaknesses that were unresolved as of December 31, 2014, as indicated in the following table.

Although these new and previously uncorrected weaknesses do not individually or collectively constitute a material weakness or a significant deficiency for the purposes of financial reporting, the corporation's overall confidence in the security and protection of its sensitive financial information and valuable resources will unfortunately remain limited until these identified issues are thoroughly resolved and remediated.

original_chunks: James Male, Andrew Bridge, Steve Warren and Paul Goslin died when the yacht they were sailing, Cheeki Rafiki, capsized in the North Atlantic.
Prosecutors at Winchester Crown Court said yacht manager Douglas Innes failed to have the vessel inspected before the journey.
Mr Innes, of Stormforce Coaching, denies four counts of manslaughter by gross negligence.
The 42-year-old, of Whitworth Crescent, Southampton, also denies a charge of not ensuring the vessel was operated safely.

Prosecutor Nigel Lickley QC also outlined to the court how the yacht had been given a category 2 code, which meant it was only authorised to be used commercially up to 60 miles away from a "safe haven".
The code certificate had expired shortly before the tragedy, he added.
The men were returning from Antigua Sailing Week to Southampton when the vessel overturned in May 2014.

The court was told that after receiving an urgent email from Andrew Bridge on board, Mr Innes, who was in a pub, did not contact the coastguard but went to another pub where Mr Bridge reported the situation had worsened.
Mr Innes returned home, called the coastguard and emailed the crew suggesting they check the bolts of the keel.
Mr Lickley noted it was a "tragedy" that they later found several bolts had failed or broken, causing the keel to detach from the yacht.
He said: "Some had failed and were broken and had been for some time," before the yacht left the UK in October 2013.

Skipper Mr Bridge, 22, from Farnham in Surrey, Mr Male, 22, from Romsey, Hampshire, Mr Warren, 52, from Bridgwater in Somerset and Mr Goslin, 56, from West Camel in Somerset, died after the yacht lost its keel over 700 miles from Nova Scotia in Canada.
The yacht was found by a container ship on 17 May, two days after Mr Bridge's urgent email, with its life raft still on board.
Mr Lickley told jurors the keel's loss would have caused a "rapid capsize" and the men on deck would have been "jettisoned" into the water while those inside would have been trapped.

He added: "What is clear from two of the emergency beacons used by Andrew Bridge and James Male is that they may have survived for some time, most probably in the water, that is until they were lost too."
The US Coastguard was criticised for calling off its search after two days.
However, following protests from family and friends, and intervention by the British government, the search was restarted and the boat was discovered, the court heard.
The trial continues.
