original_chunks: The Information Quality Act (IQA) requires the Office of Management and Budget to create guidelines ensuring the quality, objectivity, utility, and integrity of federal agency information.

As part of our long-term examination of the quality of federal information, under the Comptroller General's authority, we reviewed how the act was implemented by the National Agricultural Statistics Service (NASS), and assessed the transparency of the documentation supporting its Census of Agriculture.
NASS is part of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).
NASS met its procedural responsibilities and reporting requirements under OMB's guidelines for implementing the act.
For example, NASS drafted its own implementation guidance, and developed a mechanism allowing affected parties to request the correction of information they believe is of poor quality.
As a result of our review, NASS has also taken steps to better document the criteria it uses to evaluate data users' input on the content of the Census of Agriculture.
Enhanced documentation could further improve the transparency of census data products.
The nine key products from the 2002 Census we examined lacked, among other things, discussions of any data limitations.

This is contrary to NASS's own guidelines for ensuring transparency, which stress the importance of describing the methods, data sources, and other items to help users understand how the information was designed and produced.

Although NASS complied with OMB's requirement to establish a mechanism under IQA to address correction requests, NASS has not documented its approach for handling correction requests not filed under IQA (NASS handles these correction requests using an existing, informal method).
Agency officials indicated data users have been satisfied with NASS's response to these requests.

However, because NASS does not document its informal procedures for handling correction requests and lacks a recordkeeping system to log and track them, NASS could not provide us with specific data on the number of such requests it has handled, the nature of those requests, and whether and how they were addressed.

original_chunks: The number of aliens detained each year by DHS's (DHS) U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) rose from about 95,000 in fiscal year 2001 to 283,000 in 2006.
The care and treatment of these detained aliens is a significant challenge to ICE.
GAO was asked to assess how ICE implemented its alien detention standards.
GAO reviewed (1) detention facilities' compliance with ICE's detention standards, (2) ICE's compliance review process, and (3) how detainee complaints regarding conditions of confinement are handled.
To conduct its work, GAO reviewed DHS documents, interviewed program officials, and visited 23 detention facilities that differed in size, type, and location.

GAO's observations at 23 alien detention facilities showed systemic telephone system problems at 16 of 17 facilities that use the pro bono telephone system, but no pattern of noncompliance for other standards GAO reviewed.

At facilities relying on ICE's detainee pro bono telephone system, GAO had major trouble reaching consulates, pro bono legal providers, or the DHS Office of the Inspector General (OIG) complaint hotline.
Monthly performance data from the phone system contractor show that the successful connection rate via the detainee pro bono telephone system never exceeded 74 percent.
ICE officials said the phone contract oversight was limited.
In June 2007, ICE asked the OIG to audit the contract, alleging the contractor failed to meet the terms and conditions.
GAO found deficiencies that varied by facility, but they did not suggest a consistent noncompliance pattern.
These deficiencies involved medical care, use of hold rooms, use of force, food service, recreational opportunities, access to legal materials, facility grievance procedures, and overcrowding.
ICE's annual compliance reviews also found deficiencies like those GAO identified.
However, insufficient internal controls and weaknesses in ICE's compliance review process resulted in ICE's failure to identify telephone system problems at most facilities GAO visited.

ICE's inspection worksheet used by its detention facility reviewers did not require that a reviewer confirm that detainees are able to make successful connections through the detainee pro bono telephone system.
Detainee complaints can be submitted to several public and private organizations.
Detainee complaints mostly involved legal access, conditions of confinement, property issues, human and civil rights, medical care, and employee misconduct at the facility.
The primary way for detainees to file complaints is to contact the OIG.
OIG investigates the most serious complaints and refers the remainder to other DHS components.

original_chunks: Manipulating image visual attributes via human-written text is highly challenging.

On the one hand, models have to learn the manipulation
without the ground truth of the desired output.
On the other hand, models must handle natural language ambiguity.
Previous studies often require either full image descriptions or heavily annotated caption datasets.

In this
work, we propose a novel unsupervised approach, based on image-to-image
translation, that alters the attributes of a given image through a command-like
sentence such as "change the hair color to black".
In contrast to state-of-the-art methods, our model doesn't need annotated datasets or full attribute descriptions, only those to be modified.

Our proposed model disentangles the
image content from the visual attributes, and it learns to modify the latter
using the textual description, before generating a new image from the content
and the modified attribute representation.

Because text might be inherently
ambiguous (blond hair may refer to different shadows of blond, e.g. golden, icy, sandy), our method generates multiple stochastic translations of the same image.
Experiments show the model achieves promising results on two large-scale datasets: CelebA and CUB.

We believe our
approach will pave the way to new avenues of research combining textual and
speech commands with visual attributes.

original_chunks: Very deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have substantially improved performance on various image restoration tasks.

However, this comes at a price
of increasing computational burden, hence limiting their practical usages.
We note that some corrupted image regions are inherently easier to restore than others, since distortion and content vary across an image.
To exploit this, we present Path-Restore, a multi-path CNN with a pathfinder that dynamically selects the appropriate route for each image region.

We train the
pathfinder using reinforcement learning with a difficulty-regulated reward.
This reward reflects performance, complexity, and "the difficulty of restoring a region".
We also investigate a policy mask for jointly processing all image regions.

We conduct experiments on denoising and mixed
restoration tasks.

The results show that our method achieves comparable or
superior performance to existing approaches with less computational cost.
In particular, Path-Restore works well for real-world denoising, where noise distribution varies across regions within a single image.

Compared to the
state-of-the-art RIDNet, our method achieves comparable performance and runs
2.7x faster on the realistic Darmstadt Noise Dataset.

original_chunks: Deep generative models can learn latent representations and complex temporal dependencies in time series.

This
work introduces the Smoothness-Inducing Sequential Variational Auto-Encoder
(SISVAE) for reliable estimation and anomaly detection in
multidimensional time series.

We use a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) with a Recurrent Neural Network
to extract latent temporal patterns for both generation and inference.

Specifically, our model parameterizes mean and variance for each time-stamp
with flexible neural networks, resulting in a non-stationary model that can
work without the assumption of constant noise as commonly made by existing
Markov models.

However, such a flexibility may cause the model fragile to
anomalies.
For robust density estimation that also supports detection, we introduce a smoothness-inducing prior over possible estimates.

The proposed prior works as a regularizer that places penalty at
non-smooth reconstructions.
Our model can be trained efficiently with a newly developed stochastic gradient variational Bayes estimator.

In particular, we study two
decision criteria for anomaly detection: reconstruction probability and
reconstruction error.

We show the effectiveness of our model on both synthetic
datasets and public real-world benchmarks.

original_chunks: Public assistance programs make millions of dollars in improper payments every year.
Some of these improper payments occur because state and local agencies that run the programs lack adequate, timely information to determine recipients' eligibility for assistance.
Without such information exchange, federal and state tax dollars may be unnecessarily spent on benefits for the same individuals and families in multiple states.
In 1997, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) launched a project to help states share eligibility information.

The Public Assistance Reporting Information System (PARIS) interstate match lets states share public assistance information, including Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) and Food Stamps, to identify individuals or families who may be receiving benefits in more than one state at the same time.
Officials in nearly all 16 participating states and the District of Columbia reported that PARIS has helped identify improper TANF, Medicaid, or Food Stamp payments.
Despite its success, the project has several limitations.
First, the opportunity to detect improper duplicate payments is not as great as it could be because only one-third of the states participate.
Second, participating states lack adequate protocols or guidelines for essential interstate communication.
As a result, some states have reported critical problems, such as difficulty determining whether an individual identified in a match is actually receiving benefits in another state.
Third, state administrators for the TANF, Medicaid, and Food Stamp programs have not always placed adequate priority on using PARIS matches to identify recipients who are living in other states.
As a result, individuals may continue to receive or have benefits paid on their behalf in more than one state even after they were identified through the matching process.
Finally, because the PARIS match only identifies people after they are already on the rolls, it cannot help states prevent improper payments in the first place.

original_chunks: Finally, he became prime minister.
Although he won three general elections in a row, the Whitlam government’s dismissal after the budget impasse haunted Fraser for life and eclipsed his achievements.
As prime minister from 1975 to 1983, Fraser was widely viewed as patrician, remote, and domineering—even by some supporters.
Dubbed the "crazy grazier" by the media and an "Easter Island statue" by Labor opponent and future Labor prime minister Paul Keating, Fraser was a study in contradictions.

He was an economic conservative but a modest social reformer; a Cold War warrior and a fierce opponent of apartheid; a traditionalist with a social conscience he only gave full rein to in his later years.
John Malcolm Fraser, a rising conservative figure, was born on 21 May 1930, into a well-to-do Victorian political family.
He grew up at Nareen Station in western Victoria, then attended Melbourne Grammar School and went on to Oxford University.
He was elected to parliament in 1955 aged just 25, and the following year married Tamara Beggs, eldest daughter of another prominent farming family.
By 1966, Fraser had become minister for the army in Harold Holt's first administration.
As a rising figure in conservative politics, he sometimes overreached and followed a course not always aligned with his party.
But by 1975 he was opposition leader, confronting the radical and trouble-prone Whitlam government.

Titans of the Australian political scene in more ways than one - Fraser was just shy of Whitlam's 6ft 4in (1.93m) - the two men were key players in Australia's most controversial political moment: a constitutional crisis that led to Whitlam's dismissal by Australia's governor-general in November 1975.

This testimony presents GAO's findings on the Smithsonian's real property management and its efforts to fund facilities projects.
In addition, it describes preliminary results of GAO's ongoing work on the Smithsonian's governance challenges.

In 2005, the Government Accountability Office (GAO) determined and reported that the Smithsonian's existing financial resources were insufficient to cover its estimated $2.3 billion in anticipated facilities projects through the year 2013, consequently advising the Board of Regents to develop and implement a comprehensive funding strategy.

And while we're on the subject of Miley Cyrus... After finishing her performance of We Can't Stop in 2013, the singer was joined on stage by Robin Thicke and that's when things got a little... R-rated.
As Thicke began singing the controversial Blurred Lines, Cyrus began stroking him with a foam finger and doing her own interpretation of "twerking" in her latex beige bikini.
After Twitter melted, the singer defended it and claimed that she wanted to make history (mission accomplished) - but now it seems she regrets it.
Natia Kirkland - commonly known as Lil Mama - seemed to have got caught up in the moment when Jay-Z and Alicia Keys were performing their ode to New York, Empire State of Mind.
As the song came to a close, Kirkland who is also a native New Yorker, jumped on stage and posed next to the two superstars with Jay-Z trying his hardest to ignore her.
During a mash-up of hits in 2003, Madonna surprised the world by kissing Britney Spears onstage.
After cutting to the confused look on Justin Timberlake's face, Madonna then kissed Christina Aguilera.
At a time where both Spears and Aguilera were still trying to shake off their innocent teen-idol images, the kiss was an unforgettable VMA moment.

original_chunks: The use of land mines on the modern battlefield has been questioned in recent years, mainly due to their risk of causing accidental casualties and limiting U.S. forces' mobility.
These concerns were raised during the Persian Gulf War.

All U.S. land mines--including nonself-destructing and self-destructing, antipersonnel and antitank--were available for use in the Gulf War from U.S. land mine stockpiles, which held 19 million land mines.
U.S. forces deployed to the Gulf War theater carried over 2.2 million land mines for potential use.
U.S. military strategies included plans to deploy land mines if necessary based on the tactical situation.
According to DOD documents, no nonself-destructing or "dumb" land mines were used; approximately 118,000 self-destructing, or "smart," land mines were used.
DOD did not provide information on the effect of U.S. land mine use against the enemy.
According to U.S. service records, of the 1,364 total U.S. casualties in the Gulf War, 81, or 6 percent, were killed or injured by land mines.
Concerns about land mines raised in DOD lessons-learned and other reports included the fear of fratricide and loss of battlefield mobility.
These concerns led to the reluctance of some U.S. commanders to use land mines in areas that U.S. and allied forces might have to traverse.

original_chunks: DOD faces growing challenges in providing realistic training at installations and training ranges—on land, in the air, and at sea—because outside encroachment factors increasingly disrupt training.

These include urban growth, competition for radio frequencies or airspace, air or noise pollution, unexploded ordnance and munition components, endangered species habitat, and protected marine resources.

Building on work reported on in 2002, GAO assessed (1) the impact of encroachment on training ranges, (2) DOD's efforts to document the effect on readiness and cost, and (3) DOD's progress in addressing encroachment.

Encroachment was reported as having affected some training range capabilities, requiring workarounds--or adjustments to training events--and sometimes limiting training, at all stateside installations and major commands GAO visited.
GAO has found similar effects overseas.
In general, encroachment reduces how long ranges can be used and limits the kinds of training they can support.
As a result, units cannot train as they would fight.
Most encroachment issues come from population growth and urban development.
Because both are expected to increase, as are the speed and range of weapon systems used on training ranges, the problems are also expected to increase.

Despite DOD's concerns, the 2002 readiness data did not show that encroachment affected training readiness or costs, even though DOD's latest quarterly readiness report to Congress linked a training issue to encroachment.
While individual services are making some assessment of training requirements and limitations imposed by encroachment, comprehensive assessments remain to be done.
Likewise, complete training-range inventories have not been compiled to support interservice or joint sharing.
This raises the risk of inefficiencies, wasted time, missed opportunities, delays, and higher costs.
Also, although some services have reported higher costs because of encroachment-related workarounds for training, service data systems do not capture the costs comprehensively.

DOD has made some progress in addressing individual encroachment issues, such as implementing some short-term actions, proposing legislation to clarify the relationship between training and conservation statutes, and issuing a range sustainment directive.
But more is required for a comprehensive plan, as recommended by GAO earlier, that clearly identifies steps to be taken, goals and milestones to track progress, and required funding.

Synthetic Aperture Vector Flow Imaging (SA-VFI) can visualize complex cardiac
and vascular blood flow patterns at high temporal resolution with a large field
of view.
Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are often used for image and video recognition and classification.
Many modern CNN architectures also perform per-pixel predictions, vital for optical flow velocimetry.
This publication introduces the first CNN framework for 2D full flow field predictions from high frame rate SA ultrasound images using supervised learning.

The CNN was initially trained
using CFD-generated and augmented noiseless SA ultrasound data of a realistic
vessel geometry.

The CNN's flow field matched the ground truth with an endpoint error of 6.5% to 14.5%.

predict an accurate flow field indicating its ability for generalization.

requires advanced, computationally intensive VFI methods.

multidirectional flow.

The party had never lost a Holyrood election here.
However, that established political dynamic has now significantly changed.

Currently, both the Member of Parliament (MP) and the Member of the Scottish Parliament (MSP) are representatives from the Scottish National Party (SNP), prompting Labour members to actively strategize on how to reclaim what was historically a foundational party heartland.
Last year, this notable shift in political allegiance directly led the local party branch to officially endorse Jeremy Corbyn for the leadership position.
This time, they're not so sure.
Christina Boyd has been in the Labour Party for 30 years and is backing Owen Smith. "
We need to win back Scotland for Labour," she says. "

My primary concern, in terms of our political strategy, is specifically focused on what tangible benefits we can offer the people of Scotland, as I firmly believe that if elected as a UK government, we can significantly improve your lives with our policies and initiatives. "
I am confident that Owen Smith possesses the leadership qualities and vision required to help us achieve that crucial objective of reconnecting with and serving the Scottish electorate."
James McColgan was one of those who used to think Mr Corbyn could bring the party back to electoral success.
However, that is no longer his assessment or belief.
He too is backing Mr Smith this time around. "
I believe Owen has the capacity and broad appeal to attract and win over a broader segment of the population, including those who may not traditionally vote Labour," he states. "
That ability to broaden our support base is critically important for the party's future success and electoral viability."
However, that particular sentiment or opinion is not shared by many other individuals within the party here in this area.
Siobhan McCready holds the distinction of being the first Labour candidate to experience a loss in a Holyrood election within this traditionally Labour-voting constituency.
The SNP overturned a narrow majority of 500 in 2015 - and won by more than 8,000 votes.
Ms McCready firmly believes that Mr Corbyn, through his policies and appeal, is effectively bringing Labour's natural political allies back into the party fold. "

I'm a dedicated trade union representative," she says, standing in the shadow of a memorial that proudly celebrates the historical contributions of this area's dockyard workers, underscoring her connection to the working class. "

Every day in my role, I encounter individuals who, after many years of active union membership, had previously left the Labour Party and subsequently became disengaged from politics, but are now demonstrably returning to support us."
She thinks Mr Corbyn can help win Scotland back for Labour. "

He offers a form of credible leadership and a genuine chance for the Labour Party to authentically return to its foundational core principles, consistently advocating for the interests of ordinary working-class individuals."

Despite his supporters representing a minority within the local party membership, she was ultimately outvoted when the party officially selected its candidate for this contest, with Mr Smith narrowly receiving the nomination this time.

Among those Scottish local parties that officially declared a candidate in this significant leadership contest, the clear majority, specifically 23 of them, publicly expressed their support for Mr Corbyn.
In comparison, Mr Smith has secured 16 official endorsements from local parties.
However, looking at the overall picture across the entire United Kingdom, Mr Corbyn's lead over his challenger, Owen Smith, is considerably far higher in terms of total support.
He has the backing of 285, compared with Mr Smith's 53.

MSP Neil Findlay, who is widely recognized as Mr Corbyn's most vocal and prominent Scottish supporter, explicitly states that the Labour leader enjoys "very good support" among Scotland's significantly growing party membership. "

We successfully picked up nominations which were previously with Yvette Cooper and Andy Burnham during the 2015 leadership contest," he informed BBC Scotland directly from London, where he has been actively helping Mr Corbyn prepare for his upcoming visit to Scotland.
Across the UK, many on the left of politics who had previously left the Labour party, are now getting behind Mr Corbyn.
Former Respect MP George Galloway wants back into the party.
The renowned filmmaker Ken Loach, who previously founded his own distinct political party in England, is now actively speaking at numerous pro-Corbyn events, lending his support.
But is that happening in Scotland too?
Colin Fox, representing the political alliance RISE, firmly believes that there is a significant impediment preventing this from fully occurring in Scotland. "
Jeremy Corbyn's unwavering opposition to the concept of Scottish independence is undoubtedly his greatest political vulnerability and obstacle here in Scotland," Fox asserts.

The Labour Party's membership in Scotland has not experienced the same substantial growth trajectory that has been observed down south in England, primarily because he stands firmly opposed to what many Scots view as our fundamental right to self-determination."
Scottish Labour's top team is split.
The current leader, Kezia Dugdale, has publicly declared her support for Owen Smith in the leadership contest.
She says Jeremy Corbyn can't win a UK general election.
Her deputy Alex Rowley disagrees.
He's backing Mr Corbyn - and has criticised those who tried to oust him, including Ian Murray, Labour's only Scottish MP and a Dugdale ally.
Consequently, rumours of a potential split or factional divide within the Scottish Labour Party have begun to circulate widely.
The question then arises: could such a significant party split potentially happen here in Scotland?
She says no. "

When you believe in the Labour Party like I and so many people do, when you believe in that collective...whilst I hear a lot of talk about that I think everybody is ultimately and totally committed to the cause of the Labour movement."
That's a view both Jeremy Corbyn and Owen Smith have expressed too.
Tonight, both leaders will have the opportunity to directly address and engage with voters and party members here in Scotland, presenting their respective visions.

original_chunks: We consider hybrid parallelism, combining Data Parallelism (DP) and Model Parallelism (MP), to scale distributed training of large recommendation models.
We propose Dynamic Communication Thresholding (DCT), a framework to improve communication efficiency in hybrid training.

DCT filters the entities to be communicated across the network
through a simple hard-thresholding function, allowing only the most relevant
information to pass through.
DCT compresses parameter gradients sent to the parameter server during model synchronization to optimize DP communication.

The threshold is updated only once every few thousand iterations to reduce the
computational overhead of compression.
DCT integrates a novel method to compress activations and gradients during forward and backward propagation for efficient MP communication.

This is done by identifying and updating only the most relevant neurons of the
neural network for each training sample in the data.

We evaluate DCT on
publicly available natural language processing and recommender models and
datasets, as well as recommendation systems used in production at Facebook.
DCT achieves at least $100\times$ and $20\times$ reduction in communication during DP and MP, respectively.

The algorithm has been deployed in production, and it improves
end-to-end training time for a state-of-the-art industrial recommender model by
37\%, without any loss in performance.

original_chunks: Several deep convolutional neural networks were introduced for time-series classification and class-imbalance tasks.
However, these models performed worse and even failed to identify the minority class in an imbalanced temporal sequences dataset.
Because majority and minority classes are treated equally, minority samples may challenge temporal deep learning classifiers.

Until recently, there were few works applying deep learning on
imbalanced time-series classification (ITSC) tasks.

Here, this paper aimed at
tackling ITSC problems with deep learning.

An adaptive cost-sensitive learning
strategy was proposed to modify temporal deep learning models.
With the proposed strategy, classifiers could automatically assign misclassification penalties to each class.
In the experimental section, the proposed method modified five neural networks.
The models were evaluated with six metrics on a large-scale, real-world, imbalanced time-series dataset.
Each network was also evaluated alone and with several mainstream data samplers.

Experimental results illustrated that the proposed cost-sensitive
modified networks worked well on ITSC tasks.

Compared to other methods, the
cost-sensitive convolution neural network and residual network won out in the
terms of all metrics.

Consequently, the proposed cost-sensitive learning
strategy can be used to modify deep learning classifiers from cost-insensitive
to cost-sensitive.

Those cost-sensitive convolutional networks can be
effectively applied to address ITSC issues.

original_chunks: Recent advances now let new satellite-based remote sensing instruments collect global Satellite Image Time Series (SITS) with high spatial and spectral detail.
These sequences are a key part of classification frameworks for producing current, reliable land-cover maps of Earth's surfaces.

More specifically, the
combination of the temporal, spectral and spatial resolutions of new SITS makes
possible to monitor vegetation dynamics.
While conventional methods like Random Forest (RF) work for SITS classification, they don't fully exploit the temporal dimension.

Conversely, some approaches that take into account the temporal dimension have
recently been tested, especially Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs).

This paper
proposes an exhaustive study of another deep learning approaches, namely
Temporal Convolutional Neural Networks (TempCNNs) where convolutions are
applied in the temporal dimension.
The goal is to evaluate TempCNNs' contribution to SITS classification quantitatively and qualitatively.

This paper proposes a set of experiments performed on one million time series
extracted from 46 Formosat-2 images.
The results indicate TempCNNs outperform RF and RNNs, the current state of the art for SITS classification.

We also highlight some differences with results
obtained in computer vision, e.g. about pooling layers.
We also share general guidance on network architecture, common regularization methods, and hyperparameters like batch size.
Lastly, we evaluate the visual fidelity of the land cover maps generated by TempCNNs.

Other governmental and nongovernmental entities play a role in immigrant integration as well.

GAO was asked to determine (1) the steps USCIS has taken to implement its integration programs and the extent to which it has assessed its grant program in particular, and (2) what federal mechanism exists to coordinate integration efforts.

Among other things, GAO examined documentation on mission objectives and performance measures on immigrant integration and conducted interviews with officials in a nongeneralizable sample of cities and community-based organizations as well as senior USCIS officials about their immigrant integration efforts.

modified_chunks: In 2009, about 39 million foreign-born people lived in the United States.
Immigrant integration is generally described as a process that helps immigrants achieve self-sufficiency, political and civic involvement, and social inclusion.

DHS's U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) actively promotes political and civic engagement among immigrants through the well-established naturalization and citizenship process, thereby fostering their full participation in American society.

The Office of Citizenship (OoC) within USCIS plays a crucial role in supporting this process, primarily by awarding competitive grants to various immigrant-serving organizations, which is further complemented by extensive outreach efforts and the provision of valuable educational resources.
Other governmental and nongovernmental entities play a role in immigrant integration as well.

GAO was asked to determine (1) the steps USCIS has taken to implement its integration programs and the extent to which it has assessed its grant program in particular, and (2) what federal mechanism exists to coordinate integration efforts.

Among other things, GAO examined documentation on mission objectives and performance measures on immigrant integration and conducted interviews with officials in a nongeneralizable sample of cities and community-based organizations as well as senior USCIS officials about their immigrant integration efforts.

USCIS has successfully implemented its immigrant integration initiatives through comprehensive outreach activities, the development and distribution of valuable educational materials, and the establishment of a robust grant program, for which specific performance measures have been put in place, although interim milestones for planned evaluations are currently lacking.

From 2008 to 2011, the Office of Citizenship (OoC) officially reported conducting over 300 significant outreach campaigns specifically designed to effectively raise awareness regarding the importance of citizenship and civic participation among immigrant communities.

Furthermore, approximately $19.8 million, which constitutes nearly half of the Office of Citizenship's (OoC) entire budget over the preceding three fiscal years, was strategically granted to various organizations dedicated to preparing immigrants for the naturalization process.

These significant grants were thoughtfully distributed to a diverse array of governmental and non-governmental bodies, including established public education systems, as well as various community and faith-based organizations dedicated to immigrant support.

The Office of Citizenship (OoC) has meticulously established various clear and measurable criteria for effectively assessing the performance of its grantees operating under its comprehensive grant program.

These measures include, for example, the number of participants enrolled in grantees citizenship instruction and naturalization preparation programs, the number of participants who passed their naturalization examinations, and the proportion of participants who received grantees services and self-reported that they naturalized during the year of the grant program.

However, USCIS has identified inherent limitations with these measures, such as that its data were incomplete in part because data were self-reported by program participants, and not all program participants reported to grantees whether they passed the naturalization examination and naturalized.

In January 2011, USCIS drafted a statement of work for a contractor to develop an evaluation plan that would allow USCIS to measure the grant programs performance and long-term impact, and this may help address these limitations.

According to official statements from USCIS, the agency did not finalize this statement of work or proceed with awarding a contract for an evaluation plan because, at that specific time, there was considerable uncertainty within the agency regarding whether it would receive the necessary appropriations in fiscal year 2011 to sustain the grant program, particularly given that the program currently lacks an authorizing statute.

Despite the passage of the final fiscal year 2011 legislation in April 2011, which explicitly permitted the allocation of funds for the grant program, USCIS subsequently did not proceed with the development of an evaluation plan as initially contemplated.

In November 2011, USCIS publicly announced its strategic plans for conducting both internal and external program evaluations during fiscal years 2012 and 2013, respectively, contingent upon the receipt of sufficient appropriations for the grant program.
However, USCIS has not yet established specific intermediate milestones that would guide these upcoming evaluations, which could impact their overall effectiveness and tracking.

Setting such crucial milestones, contingent on the availability of adequate funding, could significantly assist USCIS in improving its strategic planning efforts for these important evaluations, thereby aligning more effectively with established program management principles and best practices.

original_chunks: The United States has invested nearly $43 billion to develop, construct, and maintain the International Space Station over the last two decades.
The NASA Authorization Act of 2010 required NASA to enter into a cooperative agreement with a not-for-profit entity to manage the ISS National Laboratory and in 2011 did so with CASIS.
CASIS is charged with maximizing use of the ISS for scientific research by executing several required activities.
Recently, questions have arisen about the progress being made to implement the required activities and the impact it has had on ISS's return on the investment.
GAO was asked to report on the progress of CASIS's management of the ISS National Laboratory.
GAO assessed the extent to which (1) CASIS has implemented the required management activities, and (2) NASA and CASIS measure and assess CASIS's performance.

GAO carried out this work by reviewing the cooperative agreement between NASA and CASIS, CASIS's annual program plans, and other pertinent documentation, and by conducting interviews with officials from ISS, CASIS, and NASA.

The Center for the Advancement of Science in Space (CASIS), which manages the International Space Station (ISS) National Laboratory, has taken measures to fulfill its management obligations outlined in its cooperative agreement with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and has initiated the activities required by the NASA Authorization Act of 2010.

GAO found that CASIS established procedures for prioritizing research; assessed 206 proposals and awarded approximately $20 million in grants to 77 research projects by January 2015; and developed relationships with academic institutions, research-focused organizations, and other entities.

CASIS, however, has not been able to fulfill its responsibility in the cooperative agreement to interact with the ISS National Laboratory Advisory Committee, which NASA was statutorily required to establish under the Federal Advisory Committee Act, because NASA has yet to staff the committee as required by the NASA Authorization Act of 2008.
As a result, CASIS is not able to fulfill its responsibility in the cooperative agreement that requires it to coordinate with this committee and review any report or recommendations it originates.

CASIS has set fiscal year 2015 metrics that correspond with most of GAO's key attributes for effective performance measures (see figure below); however, NASA and CASIS did not define specific targets for these performance metrics, and NASA's annual evaluation of CASIS was not documented.
Source: GAO analysis.

| GAO-15-397 GAO's work on best practices for measuring program performance has found that performance metrics should have quantifiable targets to help assess whether goals and objectives were achieved by easily comparing projected performance and actual results.
CASIS officials informed GAO in July 2014 that setting measurable targets would be arbitrary because CASIS processes and metrics are still in development.
However, in January 2015, the Chairman of the CASIS Board of Directors informed GAO that establishing measurable targets is a key priority for the board.
CASIS, however, has yet to establish a date by which measurable targets will be developed.
Under the established metrics, NASA is required by the cooperative agreement to conduct an annual performance review of CASIS's performance.
This review is informal and not documented as ISS program officials provide the results to CASIS orally.

This approach is inconsistent with federal internal control standards, which call for information to be recorded and communicated to those who need it to manage programs, including monitoring performance and supporting future decision making.
Although NASA officials reported that they were generally satisfied with CASIS's performance, CASIS officials stated that a formal summary of the results would make the information more actionable.

In 2013, Medicare financed health care services for approximately 51 million individuals at a cost of about $604 billion.
Because fraud is deceptive, it is hard to measure how widespread it is in Medicare, though fraud still drives the program's fiscal challenges.
More generally, for fiscal year 2013, CMS estimated improper payments—some potentially fraudulent—were nearly $50 billion.
This highlights the progress made and the main steps CMS and its program integrity contractors must take to reduce Medicare fraud.

These contractors perform functions such as screening and enrolling providers, detecting and investigating potential fraud, and identifying improper payments and vulnerabilities that could lead to payment errors.
This statement is based on relevant GAO products and recommendations issued from 2004 through 2014 using a variety of methodologies.
In April 2014, GAO also received updated information from CMS on the activities in this statement related to applicable laws, regulations, and guidance.
GAO also updated its information by reviewing public documents and relevant policies and procedures.

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)—the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) agency that oversees Medicare—has made progress on several strategies GAO previously identified as helpful against Medicare fraud, but key actions to help CMS and its program integrity contractors combat fraud remain incomplete.

Provider Enrollment : The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA) authorized, and CMS has implemented, actions to strengthen provider enrollment that address past weaknesses identified by GAO and HHS's Office of Inspector General.
For instance, CMS has hired contractors to verify whether providers and suppliers have valid licenses and operate from legitimate locations.
CMS has also engaged a contractor to perform fingerprint-based criminal history checks for high-risk providers and suppliers.

CMS could further strengthen provider enrollment by issuing a rule requiring additional disclosures from providers and suppliers and by setting core elements for their compliance programs, as authorized by PPACA.
Prepayment and Postpayment Claims Review : Medicare uses prepayment review to deny claims that should not be paid and postpayment review to recover erroneous payments.
GAO has found that increased use of prepayment edits could help prevent improper Medicare payments.
For example, prior GAO work identified millions of dollars of payments inconsistent with selected coverage and payment policies and therefore improper.
Postpayment reviews are also vital to identify and recover improper payments.

In 2011, GAO recommended improved oversight of the information systems analysts use for postpayment review, and in 2013, GAO recommended improved oversight of the contractors performing those reviews.
CMS has addressed some of these recommendations.
Addressing Identified Vulnerabilities : To manage the program effectively and help combat fraud, it is critical to have mechanisms to address vulnerabilities that could cause improper payments.
However, GAO work has shown weaknesses in CMS's processes to address such vulnerabilities, placing the Medicare program and its beneficiaries at risk.

For example, GAO has made multiple recommendations to CMS to remove Social Security numbers from beneficiaries' Medicare cards to help prevent identity theft, and, while HHS agreed with these recommendations, the department also reported that CMS could not proceed with the changes for a variety of reasons, including funding limitations.
Thus, to date, CMS has not taken action on these recommendations.
GAO has work underway addressing these key strategies, including assessing the potential use of electronic-card technologies to help reduce Medicare fraud.
GAO is also examining the extent to which CMS's information system can prevent and detect the continued enrollment of ineligible or potentially fraudulent providers in Medicare.
GAO is also reviewing CMS's oversight of program integrity efforts for prescription drugs and examining CMS's oversight of some contractors that perform postpayment claim reviews.
These studies are focused on additional actions for CMS that could help the agency more systematically reduce potential fraud in the Medicare program.

original_chunks: Existing predictive frameworks can handle Euclidean structured data, like brain images, but may struggle with geometric non-Euclidean data such as brain networks.

Besides, these are rooted the sample
selection step in using Euclidean or learned similarity measure between
vectorized training and testing brain networks.
Such sample connectomic representation may include irrelevant and redundant features that could mislead the training sample selection process.
This approach fails to leverage and retain the topology of the brain connectome.

To overcome this major
drawback, we propose Residual Embedding Similarity-Based Network selection
(RESNets) for predicting brain network evolution trajectory from a single
timepoint.

RESNets first learns a compact geometric embedding of each training
and testing sample using adversarial connectome embedding network.

This reduces the high-dimensionality of brain networks while preserving their
topological properties via graph convolutional networks.

In the next step, to calculate the similarity between subjects, we introduce the concept of a connectional brain template (CBT), a fixed network reference, where we further represent each training and testing network as a deviation from the reference CBT in the embedding space.

As such, we select the most similar training subjects to the
testing subject at baseline by comparing their learned residual embeddings with
respect to the pre-defined CBT.
After selecting optimal training samples at baseline, we average their corresponding brain networks at follow-up timepoints to predict the evolution trajectory of the testing network.

Our
experiments on both healthy and disordered brain networks demonstrate the
success of our proposed method in comparison to RESNets ablated versions and
traditional approaches.

original_chunks: Transfer reinforcement learning improves sample efficiency on unseen tasks by leveraging experience from earlier tasks.

We consider the setting where all tasks (MDPs) share the same
environment dynamic except reward function.

In this setting, the MDP dynamic is
a good knowledge to transfer, which can be inferred by uniformly random policy.
However, trajectories from a uniformly random policy do not improve the policy, substantially reducing sample efficiency.
Instead, we show that the binary MDP dynamic can be inferred from trajectories collected under any policy, removing the need for a uniformly random policy.

As the binary MDP
dynamic contains the state structure shared over all tasks we believe it is
suitable to transfer.
Based on this observation, we introduce a method that infers the binary MDP dynamic online while using it to guide state embedding learning for transfer to new tasks.
We keep state embedding learning separate from policy learning.
As a result, the learned state embedding is task- and policy-agnostic, making it well suited for transfer learning.

In addition, to facilitate the exploration over the state space, we
propose a novel intrinsic reward based on the inferred binary MDP dynamic.

Our
method can be used out-of-box in combination with model-free RL algorithms.

We
show two instances on the basis of \algo{DQN} and \algo{A2C}.
Extensive experiments demonstrate the advantages of our proposed method across a range of transfer learning tasks.

original_chunks: Modern video captioning deep learning is usually built on an encoder-decoder framework.

In encoder, visual features are extracted with 2D/3D Convolutional
Neural Networks (CNNs) and a transformed version of those features is passed to
the decoder.

The decoder uses word embeddings and a language model to map
visual features to natural language captions.

Due to its composite nature, the
encoder-decoder pipeline provides the freedom of multiple choices for each of
its components, e.g the choices of CNNs models, feature transformations, word
embeddings, and language models etc.

Component selection can have drastic
effects on the overall video captioning performance.
To date, the literature lacks a coordinated study of this issue.
This work addresses the gap with the first comprehensive empirical analysis of how each key component impacts a modern video captioning pipeline.

We
perform extensive experiments by varying the constituent components of the
video captioning framework, and quantify the performance gains that are
possible by mere component selection.
Using the MSVD dataset, we show that careful component selection can yield major gains without changing the pipeline.
These findings should inform future work in the rapidly expanding field of video captioning.

This testimony discusses the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) progress and challenges in harmonizing international aviation security standards and practices and facilitating compliance with international standards.
This testimony is based on reports GAO issued from April 2007 through June 2010, and ongoing work examining foreign airport assessments.

For this work, GAO gathered information from DHS and TSA, interviewing TSA officials, foreign aviation authorities, representatives from international bodies like ICAO, and industry associations regarding harmonization and TSA airport assessment challenges.

In the wake of the December 2009 terrorist incident, DHS and TSA have strived to enhance ongoing efforts to harmonize international security standards and practices through increased global outreach, coordination of standards and practices, use of enhanced technology, and assessments of foreign airports.
For example, in 2010 the Secretary of Homeland Security attended five regional summits to build international consensus on aviation security.

In addition, DHS and TSA have coordinated with foreign governments to harmonize air cargo security practices to address the statutory mandate to screen 100 percent of air cargo transported on U.S.-bound passenger aircraft by August 2010, which TSA aims to meet by 2013.

Following the December 2009 incident, the Secretary of Homeland Security encouraged other nations to deploy advanced imaging technology (AIT), which screeners use to detect anomalies like explosive devices by generating a visual representation of a passenger's physique.

Furthermore, after the October 2010 air cargo bomb incident, TSA implemented additional security protocols to enhance air cargo safety.
To ensure adherence to international security standards, TSA evaluates foreign airports' security measures, consistent with ICAO's international aviation security standards.

In 2007, GAO reported that TSA did not consistently monitor or document host governments' progress in addressing identified security deficiencies during foreign airport evaluations and recommended improved tracking and documentation.

DHS and TSA have made progress in their efforts to enhance international aviation security through these harmonization efforts and related foreign airport assessments; however, a number of key challenges, many of which are beyond DHS's control, exist.
For example, harmonization depends on the willingness of sovereign nations to voluntarily coordinate their aviation security standards and practices.
In addition, foreign governments may view aviation security threats differently, and therefore may not consider international aviation security a high priority.
Resource availability, which is a particular concern for developing countries, as well as legal and cultural factors may also affect nations' security enhancement and harmonization efforts.

original_chunks: USPS's declining revenues are no longer sufficient to cover its costs.
USPS has reduced service hours at many post offices and expanded use of post office alternatives, including CPUs.
Although CPUs can provide important benefits, the number of CPUs has fallen from 5,290 in fiscal year 2002 to 3,619 in fiscal year 2011.

This report discusses: (1) how CPUs support USPS's post office network, (2) USPS's revenue from CPUs and compensation to them from fiscal years 2007 to 2011, and (3) challenges USPS might face if it increases CPU use.
GAO analyzed USPS data on CPU locations, revenues, compensation, and hours of operation as well as on post office locations and hours of operation.
GAO interviewed CPU owners and USPS staff in charge of managing CPUs.

Although contract postal units (CPUs) have declined in number, their nationwide presence in urban and rural areas supplements the U.S. Postal Service's (USPS) network of post offices by providing additional locations and hours of service.
More than 60 percent of CPUs are in urban areas where they can provide customers nearby alternatives for postal services when they face long lines at local post offices.
More than half of CPUs are within two miles of the nearest post office.
Urban CPUs are, on average, closer to post offices than rural CPUs.
CPUs are also sometimes located in remote or fast-growing areas where post offices are not conveniently located or may not be cost-effective.
CPUs further supplement post offices by offering extended hours of service.
On average, CPUs are open 54 hours per week, compared to 41 hours for post offices.
A greater proportion of CPUs than post offices are open after 6 p.m. and on Sundays.
These factors are important as USPS considers expanding the use of post office alternatives to cut costs and maintain access to its products and services.

Total USPS revenues from CPUs fell from fiscal years 2007 to 2011, while USPS's compensation to them increased during this period; nonetheless, CPUs generated high revenues relative to USPS's compensation to CPUs.
Declines in mail volumes and the number of CPUs drove revenues down 9 percent, from $672 million to $611 million from fiscal years 2007 to 2011.

USPS total compensation to CPUs increased 6 percent during this period, from $76 million to $80 million; however, after increasing from fiscal year 2007 to 2008, compensation decreased every fiscal year from 2008 to 2011.
According to USPS officials, the overall increase was due to higher compensation to individual CPUs and a decrease in the number of less expensive CPUs.
In fiscal year 2011, after compensating CPUs, USPS retained 87 cents of every dollar of CPU revenue.
USPS has a target to retain 80 cents for every dollar in revenue for individual CPUs.
USPS did not meet this target at many individual CPUs-- especially ones in rural areas.

In fact, 49 percent of CPUs that USPS compensates a fixed amount regardless of their sales in small-town rural areas-- where CPUs may serve as the de facto post office--generated less postal revenue than the CPUs received in compensation from USPS.
CPU revenues and compensation are important factors as USPS seeks a more sustainable cost structure.
Limited interest from potential partners, competing demands on USPS staff resources, and changes to USPS's retail network may pose challenges to USPS's use of CPUs.
USPS has no current plans to strategically increase the number of CPUs as part of its retail network transformation.
However, some district USPS staff charged with identifying the need for CPUs believe a larger role for CPUs is possible.

Nevertheless, USPS may face limited interest from potential partners as many may not want to operate CPUs because of concerns over CPU contract requirements such as space requirements and prohibitions on selling products and services that compete with USPS.
Many USPS district retail managers we spoke with in charge of opening CPUs said that finding partners to operate CPUs could be difficult.
Furthermore, many of these managers said that they now have fewer staff and less time and, as a result, do not have the resources to manage opening CPUs to meet the need they have identified.

original_chunks: Over $18 billion has been appropriated to the Joint Improvised Explosive Device (IED) Defeat Organization (JIEDDO) to address the improvised explosive device (IED) threat, and there is widespread consensus that this threat will continue to be influential in future conflicts.

DOD established the Joint Improvised Explosive Device Defeat Organization (JIEDDO) in 2006 to lead, advocate, and coordinate all DOD actions in support of the combatant commanders and their respective joint task forces efforts to defeat IEDs.

This report, one in a series on JIEDDOs management and operations, addresses the extent to which DOD (1) has provided a comprehensive counter-IED strategic plan including measurable objectives that determine the effectiveness of efforts across DOD to combat IEDs, and (2) has identified counter-IED initiatives and activities, and coordinated these efforts.

To address these objectives GAO reviewed counter-IED efforts from fiscal years 2006 through 2011, reviewed and analyzed relevant strategic-planning documents, collected and reviewed data identifying DOD counter-IED efforts, and met with DOD and service officials.

Because DOD Directive 2000.19E designated JIEDDO to lead, advocate, and coordinate all DOD activities to defeat improvised explosive devices (IED), it was directed in February 2006 to develop DODs counter-IED strategic plan.

As previously recommended by GAO, JIEDDO has made several attempts to develop such a plan, but its strategic-planning actions have not followed leading strategic-management practices or have since been discontinued.
For example, JIEDDOs 2007 strategic plan did not contain a means of measuring its performance outcomesa leading strategic-management practice.
Also, although JIEDDOs 20092010 strategic plan included performance measures, it stopped using them after concluding they did not match the organizations goals.

Even though DOD assigned JIEDDO responsibility for developing the counter-IED strategic plan, DOD has not translated the departments mission of eliminating IEDs as a weapon of strategic influence into concrete, actionable goals and objectives.
JIEDDO issued a new counter-IED strategic plan in January 2012; however, the new plan does not apply to all other counter-IED efforts departmentwide, only to those managed by JIEDDO.
Thus, relying only on JIEDDOs updated strategic plan is insufficient to establish the basis for evaluating the effectiveness of all counter-IED efforts across DOD.
Further, as JIEDDO implements its plan, it will continue to have trouble measuring effectiveness until DOD sets results-oriented goals to go with its general mission objective.
Without actionable goals and objectives established by DOD, JIEDDO and other DOD components cannot tie individual performance measures to DODs desired outcomes.

As a result, DOD and external stakeholders will not have a comprehensive, data-driven assessment of whether their counter-IED efforts are meeting DODs mission, and they will not know overall effectiveness or how resources support that mission.
DOD has not identified all its counter-IED initiatives and activities, limiting its ability to coordinate them effectively across DOD.

To build a comprehensive database, consistent with a GAO recommendation, JIEDDO used at least three systems to collect and log complete information on DODs counter-IED efforts, but it shut each one down due to problems such as insufficient timeliness, inadequate coverage, or cost.
For example, beginning in 2009, JIEDDO pursued the Technology Matrix as a possible counter-IED database intended to cover all DOD efforts.
However, JIEDDO ended use of the Technology Matrix as a database because DOD did not require all relevant organizations to submit information, leaving it insufficiently comprehensive.
Without an automated means for comprehensively capturing data on all counter-IED efforts, the military services may be unaware of potential overlap, duplication, or fragmentation.

For instance, GAO found six systems that DOD components developed to emit energy to neutralize IEDs, and DOD spent about $104 million on these efforts, which could be duplicative because the military services did not collaborate.
Given the lack of a DOD-wide counter-IED database, other efforts may be overlapping.

original_chunks: Modern Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) are large, complex, and interconnected, making them vulnerable to cyberattacks.
Traditional detection methods are often insufficient for the dynamic and complex nature of CPSs.
Conversely, networked sensors and actuators produce vast data streams that can be continuously monitored for intrusions.

Unsupervised machine learning
techniques can be used to model the system behaviour and classify deviant
behaviours as possible attacks.
This study presents a new Generative Adversarial Networks-based Anomaly Detection (GAN-AD) method designed for complex networked Cyber-Physical Systems.

We used LSTM-RNN in our GAN to capture the distribution of the
multivariate time series of the sensors and actuators under normal working
conditions of a CPS.

Instead of treating each sensor's and actuator's time
series independently, we model the time series of multiple sensors and
actuators in the CPS concurrently to take into account of potential latent
interactions between them.

Our GAN employs both its generator and discriminator components, using the GAN-trained discriminator with discrepancies between generator-reconstructed data and real samples, to identify potential anomalies in the complex CPS.

We used our GAN-AD to distinguish
abnormal attacked situations from normal working conditions for a complex
six-stage Secure Water Treatment (SWaT) system.

Experimental results showed
that the proposed strategy is effective in identifying anomalies caused by

Motivated by recent advances of
self-supervision for representation learning in natural language processing and
computer vision, self-supervised learning has been recently studied to leverage
unlabeled graph-structured data.

However, employing self-supervision tasks as
auxiliary tasks to assist a primary task has been less explored in the
literature on graphs.
We introduce a novel self-supervised auxiliary learning framework to enhance graph neural network learning.
This work is the first to show that meta-path prediction is a beneficial self-supervised auxiliary task for heterogeneous graphs.
Our method learns a primary task with various auxiliary tasks to improve generalization performance.
The proposed method finds an effective combination of auxiliary tasks and automatically balances them to improve the primary task.

Our methods can be applied to any graph neural network in a
plug-in manner without manual labeling or additional data.

Also, it can be
extended to any other auxiliary tasks.

Our experiments demonstrate that the
proposed method consistently improves the performance of node classification
and link prediction.

original_chunks:
Applications of reinforcement learning (RL) to stabilization problems of real
systems are restricted since an agent needs many experiences to learn an
optimal policy and may determine dangerous actions during its exploration.

If
we know a mathematical model of a real system, a simulator is useful because it
predicates behaviors of the real system using the mathematical model with a
given system parameter vector.

We can collect many experiences more efficiently
than interactions with the real system.
However, accurately identifying the system parameter vector is difficult.
If there is an identification error, simulator-generated experiences may degrade the learned policy's performance.

Thus, we propose a practical RL algorithm that consists of two
stages.
At the first stage, we choose multiple system parameter vectors.
Next, we prepare a mathematical model for each system parameter vector, calling each model a virtual system.
We compute optimal Q-functions for multiple virtual systems using the continuous deep Q-learning algorithm.
In the second stage, we represent the real system's Q-function as a linear approximation whose basis functions are the optimal Q-functions learned in the first stage.
The agent then learns the Q-function online by interacting with the real system.
By numerical simulations, we show the usefulness of our proposed method.

original_chunks: Authorized employers use FBI criminal history checks to assess a person's suitability for employment or licensure.
States create criminal records, and the FBI lets other states access them for nationwide checks.
GAO was asked to assess efforts to address concerns about incomplete records, among other things.

This report addresses to what extent (1) states conduct FBI record checks for selected employment sectors and face any challenges; (2) states have improved the completeness of records, and remaining challenges that federal agencies can help mitigate; and (3) private companies conduct criminal record checks, the benefits those checks provide to employers, and any related challenges.

GAO analyzed laws and regulations used to conduct criminal record checks and assessed the completeness of records; conducted a nationwide survey, which generated responses from 47 states and the District of Columbia; and interviewed officials that manage checks from the FBI and 4 states (California, Florida, Idaho, and Washington).
GAO selected these states based on geography and other factors.

Most states responding to GAO's nationwide survey reported conducting Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) criminal history record checks for people working with vulnerable populations—such as children and the elderly—and in other sectors GAO reviewed (see fig.
below).
States that did not conduct FBI record checks said this was because the state lacked a designated agency to review check results, among other challenges.
In 2006, the Attorney General proposed allowing nongovernmental entities to also serve in this role, noting this would require considering data security and personal information protection.
States have improved the completeness of criminal history records used for FBI checks—more now include both the arrest and final disposition (e.g., a conviction)—but deficiencies remain.
Twenty states reported that more than 75 percent of their arrest records had dispositions in 2012, up from 16 states in 2006.
Incomplete records can delay checks and affect applicants seeking employment.
The Department of Justice has helped states improve record completeness through grants and other resources, but challenges remain.

For example, the FBI's Advisory Policy Board—which includes representatives from federal, state, and local criminal justice agencies—created a Disposition Task Force in 2009 to address issues regarding disposition reporting, among other things.
The task force has taken actions to better measure the completeness of state records and identify state requirements for reporting disposition information.

However, the task force has not set plans or time frames to finish its remaining goals, such as reviewing and recommending improvements to national standards for collecting and reporting disposition information.
Stakeholders GAO contacted said private companies appear to be used more for criminal history record checks because of employer demand and can offer benefits such as faster response times.
Federal agencies regulate these companies and have settled complaints, such as in cases where the wrong records were sent to employers.
Private companies can face challenges in obtaining complete and accurate records, in part because not all states make their criminal record information accessible for private companies to search.

original_chunks: Each year, tens of thousands of aliens in the United States apply for asylum, which provides refuge to those who have been persecuted or fear persecution on protected grounds.
Asylum applications are adjudicated by asylum officers in DHS's USCIS and immigration judges in DOJ's EOIR.
The Government Accountability Office (GAO) was asked to examine the asylum system.

This report examines (1) trends in asylum claims from DHS and DOJ data, (2) DHS and DOJ mechanisms for preventing and detecting asylum fraud, and (3) DHS and DOJ procedures for addressing identified asylum fraud.

GAO analyzed DHS and DOJ data on asylum applications for fiscal years 2010 through 2014, reviewed DHS and DOJ policies and procedures related to asylum fraud, and interviewed DHS and DOJ officials in Washington, D.C., Falls Church, VA, and in asylum offices and immigration courts across the country selected on the basis of application data and other factors.
Asylum applications, including principal applicants and dependents, more than doubled from 47,118 in fiscal year 2010 to 108,152 in fiscal year 2014.
As of September 2015, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has a backlog of 106,121 principal applicants, of which 64,254 have exceeded required time frames for adjudication.
USCIS plans to hire additional staff to address the backlog.
USCIS and the Department of Justice's (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) have limited capabilities to detect asylum fraud.
Firstly, despite having mechanisms for individual fraud investigations, neither USCIS nor EOIR has evaluated fraud risks across the entire asylum process, contrary to risk management best practices.
Fraudulent activities highlight vulnerabilities that could compromise asylum system integrity.

For example, a New York investigation led to charges against 30 defendants by March 2014 for alleged immigration fraud schemes; 829 applicants linked to these individuals received asylum from USCIS, and 3,709 from EOIR.
Without regular fraud risk assessments, USCIS and EOIR cannot ensure adequate controls are in place to mitigate these risks.

Second, USCIS's capability to identify patterns of fraud across asylum applications is hindered because USCIS relies on a paper-based system for asylum applications and does not electronically capture some key information that could be used to detect fraud, such as the applicant's written statement.

Asylum officers and USCIS Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) Directorate immigration officers told GAO that they can identify potential fraud by analyzing trends across asylum applications; however, they must rely on labor-intensive methods to do so.
Identifying and implementing additional fraud detection tools could enable USCIS to detect fraud more effectively while using resources more efficiently.

Third, FDNS has not established clear fraud detection responsibilities for its immigration officers in asylum offices; FDNS officers we spoke with at all eight asylum offices told GAO they have limited guidance with respect to fraud.
FDNS standard operating procedures for fraud detection are broad, not specifically addressing the asylum system's unique characteristics.

Developing asylum-specific guidance for fraud detection, in accordance with federal internal control standards, would better position FDNS officers to understand their roles and responsibilities in the asylum process.
USCIS can sometimes terminate an individual's asylum status to address identified instances of asylum fraud.
Between fiscal years 2010 and 2014, USCIS revoked 374 individuals' asylum status due to fraud.

In August 2015, USCIS adopted a target of 180 days for conducting initial reviews, in which the asylum office reviews evidence and decides whether to begin termination proceedings, when the asylee has applied for adjustment to lawful permanent resident status; however, this goal applies only to a subset of asylees and pertains to initial reviews.
Further, asylees with pending termination reviews may be eligible to receive certain federal benefits.
Establishing timeliness objectives for all pending termination reviews would help USCIS accurately determine staffing needs for the termination workload.

The presence of fraudulent activities within the asylum system clearly highlights inherent vulnerabilities that possess the potential to significantly compromise the overall integrity of the asylum system.

Second, USCIS's capability to identify patterns of fraud across asylum applications is hindered because USCIS relies on a paper-based system for asylum applications and does not electronically capture some key information that could be used to detect fraud, such as the applicant's written statement.

Third, the FDNS Directorate has not yet established clear and specific fraud detection responsibilities for its immigration officers stationed in asylum offices; indeed, FDNS officers interviewed by GAO at all eight asylum offices indicated that they currently operate with limited guidance regarding fraud detection in this context.

Furthermore, the FDNS standard operating procedures for fraud detection are currently broadly defined, and as such, they do not specifically address the unique characteristics and complexities inherent within the asylum system itself.

Developing asylum-specific guidance for fraud detection, in accordance with federal internal control standards, would better position FDNS officers to understand their roles and responsibilities in the asylum process.

Further, asylees with pending termination reviews may be eligible to receive certain federal benefits.

Establishing precise and measurable timeliness objectives for all categories of pending termination reviews would significantly assist USCIS in accurately determining the necessary staffing levels and resources required to manage the overall termination workload effectively.
