GAO analyzed DHS and DOJ data on asylum applications for fiscal years 2010 through 2014, reviewed DHS and DOJ policies and procedures related to asylum fraud, and interviewed DHS and DOJ officials in Washington, D.C., Falls Church, VA, and in asylum offices and immigration courts across the country selected on the basis of application data and other factors.

The total number of asylum applications, which includes both principal applicants and their associated dependents, more than doubled significantly, increasing from 47,118 in fiscal year 2010 to a substantial 108,152 by fiscal year 2014.
As of September 2015, the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) has a backlog of 106,121 principal applicants, of which 64,254 have exceeded required time frames for adjudication.
USCIS plans to hire additional staff to address the backlog.
USCIS and the Department of Justice's (DOJ) Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) have limited capabilities to detect asylum fraud.

Firstly, despite the existence of mechanisms designed for conducting individual fraud investigations, neither USCIS nor EOIR has undertaken a comprehensive evaluation of fraud risks across the entirety of the asylum process, which is contrary to widely recognized risk management best practices.

The presence of fraudulent activities within the asylum system clearly highlights inherent vulnerabilities that possess the potential to significantly compromise the overall integrity of the asylum system.

For example, a significant investigation conducted in New York culminated in charges being brought against 30 defendants by March 2014 for their alleged involvement in various immigration fraud schemes; notably, 829 applicants linked to these specific individuals subsequently received asylum status from USCIS, while an even larger number, 3,709, received asylum from EOIR.

Without the regular implementation of thorough fraud risk assessments, USCIS and EOIR are unable to ensure that adequate and effective controls are consistently in place to properly mitigate these identified risks.

Second, USCIS's capability to identify patterns of fraud across asylum applications is hindered because USCIS relies on a paper-based system for asylum applications and does not electronically capture some key information that could be used to detect fraud, such as the applicant's written statement.

Asylum officers and immigration officers from USCIS’s Fraud Detection and National Security (FDNS) Directorate collaboratively informed GAO that they possess the ability to identify potential instances of fraud by carefully analyzing trends across multiple asylum applications; however, they are unfortunately required to rely on highly labor-intensive, manual methods to accomplish this task.
Identifying and implementing additional fraud detection tools could enable USCIS to detect fraud more effectively while using resources more efficiently.

Third, the FDNS Directorate has not yet established clear and specific fraud detection responsibilities for its immigration officers stationed in asylum offices; indeed, FDNS officers interviewed by GAO at all eight asylum offices indicated that they currently operate with limited guidance regarding fraud detection in this context.

Furthermore, the FDNS standard operating procedures for fraud detection are currently broadly defined, and as such, they do not specifically address the unique characteristics and complexities inherent within the asylum system itself.

Developing asylum-specific guidance for fraud detection, in accordance with federal internal control standards, would better position FDNS officers to understand their roles and responsibilities in the asylum process.
In specific circumstances, USCIS possesses the authority to terminate an individual's asylum status as a direct measure to address identified and confirmed instances of asylum fraud.
During the five-year period between fiscal years 2010 and 2014, USCIS formally revoked the asylum status of 374 individuals due to documented cases of fraud.

In August 2015, USCIS adopted a target of 180 days for conducting initial reviews, in which the asylum office reviews evidence and decides whether to begin termination proceedings, when the asylee has applied for adjustment to lawful permanent resident status; however, this goal applies only to a subset of asylees and pertains to initial reviews.
Further, asylees with pending termination reviews may be eligible to receive certain federal benefits.

Establishing precise and measurable timeliness objectives for all categories of pending termination reviews would significantly assist USCIS in accurately determining the necessary staffing levels and resources required to manage the overall termination workload effectively.

original_chunks: Governments have agreed to limit global temperature rise to two degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, aiming for 1.5 degrees. "
This is a moment to celebrate," United Nations climate chief Patricia Espinosa told Reuters. "
It is also a moment to look ahead with sober assessment and renewed will over the task ahead."
The Eiffel Tower in Paris will be illuminated in green light on Friday to mark the entry into force of the historic climate pact.
Delegates from almost 200 countries are meeting in Marrakech next week to consider the way ahead beyond Paris.
The deal agreed in the French capital less than a year ago commits governments to moving their economies away from fossil fuels.

A UN review found national carbon reduction pledges fall short of the levels needed to keep global temperatures under 2C. The report found pledges from governments that have ratified the accord would see the world on track for a rise in temperatures by the end of this century of between 2.9 and 3.4 degrees C. Roger Harrabin, BBC environment analyst The Paris climate pact comes into force less than a year since it was agreed.
The last major climate deal - the Kyoto Protocol - took eight years to come into force.
Paris is the first agreement uniting rich and poor nations in a common endeavor to protect the climate.
However, national carbon emission targets are voluntary.
The UN tried a mandatory approach but countries that were failing to meet their targets simply quit.
The process of the Paris deal is binding, including a commitment for governments to keep returning to the issue to ratchet up the clean energy targets that they all agree are inadequate.
Governments that rushed to enshrine Paris in law have had one eye on the US elections.
Hilary Clinton has pledged to expand President Obama's emissions cuts.
Donald Trump wants to withdraw from the agreement.
Environmental groups and other experts have urged governments to do more.

World Bank group president Jim Yong Kim said even with the commitments made in Paris and encouraging action on the ground, "we will not meet our aspiration of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees unless we move faster and at the scale that is needed". "
As the world heads into (the meeting) in Marrakesh, we must regain the sense of urgency we felt a year ago," he said.
In Marrakech governments and parties will work on details of a "rulebook" which will measure and review global climate action.

To peak greenhouse gas emissions as soon as possible and achieve a balance between sources and sinks of greenhouse gases in the second half of this century • To keep global temperature increase "well below" 2C (3.6F) and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5C • To review progress every five years • $100 billion a year in climate finance for developing countries by 2020, with a commitment to further finance in the future.
Donald Trump has called manmade climate change "a hoax" and said he would "cancel" the Paris Agreement and other international efforts to address the issue.
He supports clean water and air, but wants to slash funding to the Environmental Protection Agency in the US.
Hillary Clinton backs the Paris deal, saying climate change is a threat to American security.
She supports stringent regulation of the energy industry and opposes expanded drilling in Alaska, but has not made the environment a central part of her campaign.

original_chunks: In 1996, Congress authorized the Recreational Fee Demonstration Program to fund improvements to visitor experience and resource protection.

Under the program, the Bureau of Land Management, the Fish and Wildlife Service, the National Park Service (within the Department of the Interior), and the Forest Service (under the U.S. Department of Agriculture) may establish, evaluate, collect, and apply fees at multiple locations, including to address repair and maintenance backlogs.
Also, sites may retain and use the fees they collect.
The Congress is now considering, through H.R. 3283, whether to make the program permanent.
A key issue is how much the agencies use the revenues they collect.
This statement considers the likely impact of H.R. 3283 on the issues GAO previously raised about the Recreational Fee Demonstration Program.

Specifically, it examines the extent to which H.R. 3283 would affect (1) federal agencies' deferred maintenance programs, (2) revenue management and allocation, and (3) interagency coordination on fee collection and use.

H.R. 3283 would provide agencies with a permanent source of funds to better address their maintenance backlog, and by making the program permanent, the act would provide agencies incentive to develop a system to track their deferred maintenance backlogs.

According to the Department of the Interior's latest estimates, the deferred maintenance backlog for the Interior agencies participating in the fee demonstration program ranges from $5.1 billion to $8.3 billion, with the Park Service alone accounting for an estimated $4 to $7 billion.
Likewise, the Forest Service estimates its overall deferred maintenance backlog at about $8 billion.

GAO's prior work on the Park Service's and Forest Service's backlog has demonstrated that neither agency has accurate and reliable information on its deferred maintenance needs and cannot determine how much of the fee demonstration revenues it spends on reducing its deferred maintenance needs.
In addition, some officials have been reluctant to fund a deferred maintenance tracking system because the program is temporary.
H.R. 3283 would reduce the on-site spending requirement to 60 percent, giving agencies more discretion in how they apply the funds.
At present, the demonstration program requires agencies to reserve at least 80 percent of collected fee revenues for on-site uses.

This requirement has helped some demonstration sites generate revenue in excess of their high-priority needs, but the high-priority needs at other sites, which did not collect as much in fee revenues, remained unmet.
GAO has suggested that the Congress consider modifying the current 80-percent on-site spending requirement to provide agencies greater flexibility in using fee revenues.

H.R. 3283 would standardize permissible fee types, create a single national pass covering recreation sites managed by different agencies, and support regional fee coordination to reach multiple nearby sites.

GAO's prior reports have demonstrated the need for more effective coordination and cooperation among the agencies to better serve visitors by making the payment of fees more convenient and equitable while reducing visitor confusion about similar or multiple fees being charged at nearby or adjacent federal recreation sites.
